Mission: Move!
M/J Comprehensive Physical Education, Grade 6/7. You are about to spend this semester as a sport scientist in training — measuring your own body, testing what works, and using the evidence to get faster, stronger and more durable. Units 1.10–1.18 · Weeks 19–36.
🚩Start Here

Open Unit 1.10: Teamwork, Sportsmanship and Respect in the Modules list and begin with the first reading. Work through each unit top to bottom — the order is deliberate. Before your first Flight Club challenge, read the Flight Club Guidelines page so you know the safety rules.

How this course works

Step 1
Read
Each unit opens with a reading built around real sport science — lessons, a Coach's Lab experiment, and a vocabulary list.
Step 2
Create
Projects and VR builds where you design something: a warm-up routine, a cardio track, a fitness station, a game.
Step 3
Move
Flight Club challenges. Short movement tasks where you collect data on your own body and submit the proof.
Step 4
Reflect
Every task ends with a data or design prompt. This is where you explain the mechanism, not just the result.

What you need

Nothing expensive. A clear space to move, closed-toe shoes with grip, water, and something to record with (phone camera or a notes app). A few challenges use a soft ball, a jump rope, or a chair — every one lists household substitutions. VR assignments use a headset where available; ask your teacher about the alternative if you do not have one.

Week 19

Teamwork and Cooperation: Multiplying Performance

Most sports — and most jobs — are played in teams. A talented individual on a team that doesn't cooperate usually loses to an average team that works together. Teamwork is a skill, just like a throw or a sprint. Sport psychologists study it the same way they study physical skills, and they have found it follows the same training rules: deliberate practice, feedback, repetition.

1
Lesson 1
What Cooperation Actually Looks Like

Cooperation is not just "being nice." It is a measurable set of behaviors that help a group reach a goal it could not reach alone:

  • Communication — clearly stating what you'll do and listening to what others say
  • Role clarity — knowing your job and trusting others to do theirs
  • Shared goal — pushing toward the same outcome, even when individual stats don't shine
  • Adaptation — adjusting the plan when the situation changes

Researchers can watch a team for ten minutes and predict its success rate by tracking these four behaviors. Teams that score high on all four win more, finish projects faster, and feel better about the work.

2
Lesson 2
Roles on a Team

Healthy teams need a mix of roles. You'll be more drawn to some than others, but in middle school you should try them all — partly to find your strengths, and partly because every role makes you better at the others.

🧭
Leader
Sets direction, makes the call when there's no time to discuss.
👂
Listener
Gathers ideas from quieter teammates and builds the plan.
🛠️
Builder
Takes the plan and executes — does the actual work.
📣
Cheerleader
Keeps energy high, picks teammates up after mistakes.
🧰
Problem-Solver
Spots when the plan isn't working and suggests a fix.
🧪Sport Science

Google ran a multi-year study called Project Aristotle, watching hundreds of teams to find what made the best ones succeed. The number one factor wasn't talent or experience. It was psychological safety — every member feels safe to speak up, admit mistakes, and propose ideas. The same finding holds in PE: a team that lets its quietest player call a play is often better than one that just listens to the loudest. Sport scientists call this distributed leadership.

3
Lesson 3
What Breaks Teams

Knowing what doesn't work is just as important as knowing what does. Common team-breakers:

  • One person dominates and doesn't pass or share decisions
  • Blaming teammates for mistakes instead of solving the problem
  • Running silent — no communication during play
  • Refusing to play a role you don't love (every position has weight)
  • Quitting after a setback instead of adapting

If you've been on a team that fell apart, you probably saw at least two of these. The good news: noticing them is the first step to choosing differently.

💡Did You Know?

U.S. Navy SEAL training emphasizes teamwork over individual ability. The strongest swimmers, fastest runners, and best shooters often fail because they cannot cooperate under stress. SEAL instructors say a slower person who keeps the team moving is more valuable than a fast person who runs alone. The mantra: the only easy day was yesterday — and we all do it together.

4
Lesson 4
Teammates of Every Background and Ability

The strongest teams are rarely the ones where everyone is the same. Sport scientists who study team performance find that teams with a range of backgrounds, body types, skill levels, and ways of thinking solve problems faster — as long as every member is treated with respect. Your job on any team is to turn that range into an advantage, not a fault line.

  • Respect different ability levels — a teammate still learning a skill is not "the weak link." Adjust the challenge so everyone contributes; that is what real cooperation looks like.
  • Respect different backgrounds — culture, language, and experience shape how people communicate and lead. Listen first and assume good intent.
  • Include on purpose — invite the quiet teammate's idea, pass to the less-confident player, and adapt activities so a teammate with a disability can fully take part.

This isn't only fair — it's effective. A team that uses everyone's strengths beats a team of similar players who shut out anyone who's different.

🌎Real-World Connection

The Paralympic Games and "unified" sports leagues — where athletes with and without intellectual disabilities compete on the same team — show that adapting an activity for different abilities doesn't lower the competition; it widens who gets to compete. Coaches report that mixed-ability teams often build the strongest chemistry of all, because cooperation, not raw talent, becomes the deciding skill.

5
Try It
Cooperation Mini-Challenges
🪢
Human Knot
Group holds hands across a circle; untangle without letting go.
🎈
Balloon Keep-Up
Keep a balloon off the floor — each person can only tap it once before someone else.
📦
Group Carry
Move an object from A to B using only feet, or only one hand each.
🤐
Silent Build
Build a tower of cups as a team — no one can talk during the build.
🌎Real-World Connection

Surgical teams, firefighting crews, airline cockpit teams, and SWAT units all run team-training drills regularly — not because the skill is new, but because cooperation is what scientists call a perishable skill. If you don't practice, you get rusty. NASA astronauts spend months in team simulations before any space mission. You're getting the same kind of practice on a smaller scale, but the principle is identical.

🔬Coach's Lab

Run an observation experiment. Watch your next team activity from the outside (or join in and reflect after). Count three things: (1) how many times teammates communicated information out loud, (2) how many times someone took on a new role mid-activity, (3) how many times anyone said something positive after a teammate's mistake. Higher counts almost always correlate with better team performance. What did your data show?

6
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Teamwork — Working with others toward a shared goal.
  • Cooperation — Adjusting your actions to fit what teammates are doing.
  • Communication — Clearly sharing information so the team can act together.
  • Role — Your specific job or position on a team.
  • Psychological safety — Team climate where every member feels safe to speak up (stretch term).
  • Distributed leadership — When different people lead at different moments based on the situation (stretch term).
  • Adaptation — Adjusting the plan based on what's actually happening.
  • Inclusion — Actively making sure teammates of every ability and background can fully take part.
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Imagine you are coaching a team that is talented but disorganized — they keep losing close games. Design a 3-week team-skills training program. Specify what you'd practice each week, why that order, and what specific measurement you'd use to track whether the program is working.

→What's Next

Next: show your teamwork in action, then carry it into sportsmanship, respect and resiliency.

Sportsmanship and Respect: The Mental Game

Winning matters. But how you compete matters more — and not just for sentimental reasons. Sport scientists who study elite athletes have found that sportsmanship and emotional control directly predict long-term performance. Athletes who can stay composed after a loss improve faster than those who can't. The mental game is a measurable, trainable skill.

1
Lesson 1
What Sportsmanship Looks Like

Good sportsmanship is a set of observable behaviors. You can list them, watch for them, and rate them:

  • Respect opponents — they're the reason competition exists
  • Respect officials — referees miss calls; arguing rarely changes them
  • Play by the rules — even when no one is watching
  • Win humbly — celebrate the result, not your opponent's defeat
  • Lose with dignity — congratulate the winner, extract the lesson

This is not just etiquette. Sportsmanship is what keeps competition fun and meaningful, season after season. Without it, sport eventually breaks down.

2
Lesson 2
The Brain Science of Losing Well

Being a good sport is hard because competition triggers strong emotions. After a loss, your brain releases stress chemicals like cortisol. After a win, you get a rush of dopamine. Both can drive you to act in ways you'd regret — taunting an opponent, blaming a teammate, slamming equipment.

Top athletes train themselves to notice these urges and choose differently. That skill is called emotional regulation, and it shows up in brain scans: experienced athletes have measurably more activity in their prefrontal cortex (the planning region) during emotional moments than untrained people do. Translation: they think before they act, even when they don't feel like it.

🧪Sport Science

When you lose a close game, the same brain regions activate as when you experience physical pain. Specifically, the anterior cingulate cortex — the part that signals social rejection and bodily pain — fires together. That's why a tough loss can feel almost like getting hurt. Sport psychologists who study Olympic athletes find that the ability to recover quickly from this state — to "lose the right way" — is one of the strongest predictors of long-term success in any sport.

3
Lesson 3
Respect Beyond Sports

The respect you build in PE is the same respect you owe people everywhere — classmates, family, future coworkers. Specific behaviors:

  • Listen actively — make eye contact, don't cut people off
  • Use names — it shows you see the person, not just a player
  • Acknowledge differences — different skills, backgrounds, and viewpoints make teams stronger
  • Stand up for teammates — especially the ones who can't always speak for themselves
💡Did You Know?

The Olympics give a specific award called the Pierre de Coubertin Medal, named after the founder of the modern Olympic Games. It's awarded to athletes who display outstanding sportsmanship — sometimes even when they LOSE the competition. Past winners have stopped during races to help injured opponents. The Olympic committee considers the medal as prestigious as gold, because they understand that sportsmanship is what makes the Games worth running.

4
Lesson 4
Peer Pressure: Positive and Negative

Competition and teams put you around other people's choices constantly, and that creates peer pressure — the influence your peers have on what you do. Peer pressure isn't automatically bad. A sport scientist treats it like any variable: it can push you in a positive or a negative direction, and naming which is which lets you use it on purpose.

⬆️
Positive peer pressure
Teammates who show up to every practice, encourage a hard rep, or insist on warming up safely. Their standard pulls yours up.
⬇️
Negative peer pressure
Pressure to skip the warm-up, taunt an opponent, play hurt, or break a rule "because everyone does." Their choice drags your standard down.

Two skills turn peer pressure to your advantage: (1) choose your training partners — you tend to rise or fall to the level of the people you train with; and (2) become the positive pressure — be the teammate whose standard everyone else wants to match.

🌎Real-World Connection

Research on youth athletes finds that a teammate's habits are one of the strongest predictors of an athlete's own choices — about training, sleep, and even sportsmanship. Coaches use this on purpose by pairing newer athletes with disciplined veterans. The influence is real and measurable; the skill is deciding which direction you let it pull you.

5
Try It
Sportsmanship Self-Check

After your next game or PE activity, run this five-item self-audit:

  1. Did I congratulate at least one opponent or teammate?
  2. Did I follow the rules even when no one was watching?
  3. How did I act after a mistake — mine or someone else's?
  4. Would my teammates say I lifted them up or brought them down?
  5. If I lost, what specifically did I learn that I can use next time?
🌎Real-World Connection

Professional leagues — including the NFL, NBA, and MLB — fine players for unsportsmanlike conduct. A single bad gesture or taunt can cost tens of thousands of dollars. The leagues do this because they have data showing sportsmanship affects fan engagement and youth participation rates. When pros behave badly, fewer kids sign up for the sport. The professional level takes sportsmanship as seriously as scoring.

🔬Coach's Lab

Track your own emotional regulation for one week. After every PE activity, game, or even a competitive board game at home, write down two things: (1) what you felt at the worst moment (anger, frustration, embarrassment), and (2) what you actually did in that moment. After 5 entries, look for patterns. Where did your behavior match the emotion (you slammed something)? Where did you regulate (you took a breath and stayed quiet)? Data, not opinion — that's where change begins.

6
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Sportsmanship — Behaving with fairness, respect, and composure in competition.
  • Respect — Treating others with consideration even during competition or disagreement.
  • Integrity — Doing the right thing even when no one is watching.
  • Humility — Winning without putting others down.
  • Emotional regulation — Managing how you respond to strong feelings (stretch term).
  • Prefrontal cortex — Brain region responsible for planning and impulse control (stretch term).
  • Fair play — Following both the written and unwritten rules of a game.
  • Peer pressure — The influence peers have on your choices — positive (raises your standard) or negative (lowers it).
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Recall a competition where you felt the strongest emotion (frustration, anger, joy, disappointment). Rate the emotion 1–10 in intensity. Then write what you actually did. Now write what you wish you had done. The gap between those two answers is the size of your emotional-regulation training opportunity. What is one specific habit that would close the gap?

→What's Next

Next: complete your sportsmanship writing assignments, then take the Flight Club Card Challenge.

Resiliency: Empathy, Perspective and Bouncing Back

Sportsmanship is how you treat people when the score is on the line. Resiliency is what happens next — how you read other people, how you decide, and how you come back when something does not go your way. Sport psychologists treat all three as trainable skills, and they measure them.

1
Lesson 1
Empathy: Reading the Other Person

Empathy is the ability to recognize what someone else is feeling and to respond in a way that fits. It is not agreeing with them and it is not feeling sorry for them — it is accurate reading followed by a useful response.

It has three moving parts:

  • Identify the feeling. Read the face, the posture, the tone, the silence. A teammate who goes quiet after a mistake is usually not calm.
  • Consider the circumstances. What else is going on for that person that you may not be able to see? The player who snapped at you may have had a terrible morning.
  • Respond. Say or do something that actually helps — which is usually far smaller than people think.

Active listening is the main tool, and it is mostly mechanical: face the person, stop doing other things, let them finish without jumping in, then say back what you heard before you add anything of your own. "So you are frustrated because you did not get subbed in" does more work than any advice you could offer.

What genuinely helps after a teammate's mistake: name it briefly and move on ("my bad too, next play"), or say nothing and stand next to them. What does not help: pretending it did not happen, over-explaining, or immediately coaching them.

🧪Sport Science

Empathy has a measurable footprint in the brain. When you watch someone else get hurt or fail, parts of your own pain and emotion networks activate — you are, in a limited but real sense, simulating their experience. Researchers have also found that empathy behaves like a skill rather than a fixed trait: it strengthens with deliberate practice and weakens with stress, fatigue and hunger. That is a practical detail for an athlete. Your capacity to be a good teammate is genuinely lower at the end of a hard practice, which is exactly when your team needs it most — so it has to be a habit, not a mood.

2
Lesson 2
Decisions That Hold Up: Multiple Perspectives

A responsible decision considers more than what you want right now. Sport psychologists teach athletes to run a decision through four lenses before committing:

  1. Me — what does this do to my health, my goals, my reputation?
  2. Them — who else is affected, and how would this look from where they are standing?
  3. The rules — what do my family's rules, my school's rules, and the law actually say?
  4. Later — how will this look in a week, a season, a year?

The second lens is the one people skip. Deliberately stating the situation from the other person's point of view — out loud, fairly, the way they would say it — changes the decision surprisingly often.

And when you have a real problem to solve, do not chase the first workable idea. Generate at least three options, predict the outcome of each for yourself and for the others involved, then choose. A first idea that works is not the same as the best outcome, and the difference between the two is usually visible only when you have written down a third option.

3
Lesson 3
Why Rules and Laws Are Worth Following

You live inside three sets of rules at once: family rules, school rules, and community laws. It is easy to read all three as restrictions. Look at what each is actually doing.

  • They protect people who cannot protect themselves in that moment — the smaller player, the pedestrian, the person who is not paying attention.
  • They make strangers able to cooperate. A game between two teams who have never met works only because both accept the same rulebook. So does a road full of drivers.
  • They distribute fairness so that outcomes come from effort and skill rather than from whoever is willing to cheat.
  • They carry real consequences — eligibility, trust, legal records — that outlast the moment that tempted you.

Following a rule when nobody is watching is the definition of integrity from Unit 1.10. The extension here is civic: a community works because most people follow most rules most of the time, including the ones they personally find inconvenient.

4
Lesson 4
Challenges and Setbacks: The Strategies That Work

Every plan in this course — every fitness goal, every training cycle — will meet a setback. Resilient people are not the ones who avoid setbacks. They are the ones with a method.

⏰
Time management
Put the session in the calendar like a class, not in the leftover time. Protect one specific slot per day rather than hoping for a free hour.
🚫
Set boundaries
Saying no to one thing is what makes another possible. Decide in advance what you will decline during a heavy week.
🎯
Set realistic goals
Scale the target to the life you actually have. A goal you hit builds momentum; a goal you miss repeatedly teaches you to stop trying.
💤
Self-care
Sleep, food, hydration and rest days are part of the plan, not a reward for finishing it. Fatigue is where most quitting happens.
📏
Scale, do not skip
A 10-minute version beats a missed session. Keeping the streak alive matters more than any single workout.
🤝
Ask for support
A coach, a parent, a friend who checks in. Athletes with a feedback partner stick to plans measurably longer than those going alone.
💡Did You Know?

Sport psychologists distinguish a lapse from a relapse. A lapse is one missed session. A relapse is abandoning the plan. What turns the first into the second is almost never the missed session itself — it is the story a person tells about it. "I missed Tuesday, so the week is ruined" is the thought that does the damage. Researchers who study habit formation find that people who simply resume the next day, without treating the gap as evidence about their character, maintain habits far longer. One missed day is a data point. Two is a pattern worth examining. Neither is a verdict.

🌎Real-World Connection

Professional teams now employ sport psychologists alongside strength coaches for exactly this reason. Athletes at the highest level lose constantly — a top hitter fails seven times out of ten, and every team but one ends its season with a defeat. What separates careers is not the frequency of setbacks but the speed of the return. Coaches call it the next-play mentality: acknowledge it, extract the lesson, reset for the next repetition. It is a trained response, and it is trained the same way a jump shot is — with reps.

🔬Coach's Lab

Run a three-option decision drill. Take a real decision you are facing this week — any decision, it does not have to be dramatic. Write down three genuinely different options, not one option and two bad ones. For each, predict the outcome for you and the outcome for everyone else affected. Now choose, and write one sentence on why. A week later, come back and check your predictions against what actually happened. Which prediction was furthest off, and what did you fail to account for? That gap is where your decision-making improves.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Empathy — Recognizing what someone else is feeling and responding in a way that fits.
  • Active listening — Facing the speaker, letting them finish, and reflecting back what you heard before responding.
  • Perspective-taking — Deliberately stating a situation the way the other person would state it (stretch term).
  • Integrity — Doing the right thing even when no one is watching.
  • Setback — An interruption to a plan - illness, a busy week, an injury, or lost motivation.
  • Lapse vs. relapse — One missed session versus abandoning the plan entirely (stretch term).
  • Next-play mentality — Acknowledge, learn, reset - the trained speed of returning after a failure (stretch term).
  • Boundary — A limit you set in advance on your time or commitments so priorities survive a busy week.
📝Weekly Reflection

Perspective prompt: Think of a recent disagreement — with a teammate, a friend, or a family member. Write the situation from their point of view, in their voice, as fairly as you can manage. Do not defend yourself inside it. Then answer: what did writing it that way change about how you see it? Finally, name one thing you could have said in the moment that would have shown empathy without giving up your own position.

→What's Next

Next: put empathy and decision-making to work in the Empathy and Decisions in Action assignment.

The Five Fitness Components: The Athlete's Toolkit

"Being in shape" means different things in different sports. A gymnast and a long-distance runner are both fit — but their fitness profiles look very different. Sport scientists have broken total fitness into five health-related components, plus several skill-related ones. Knowing which components your sport demands tells you how to train. Without this map, training is just guessing.

1
Lesson 1
The Five Health-Related Components
🫀
Cardiovascular Endurance
How long the heart and lungs can fuel sustained activity. Tested with a mile run.
💪
Muscular Strength
Maximum force produced in one effort. Tested with a max push-up or squat.
🔋
Muscular Endurance
How long muscles can keep producing force. Tested with timed plank or repeated sit-ups.
🤸
Flexibility
How far a joint can move comfortably. Tested with a sit-and-reach.
⚖️
Body Composition
Ratio of muscle, bone, water, and fat in the body. Tracked over time, not in single snapshots.
🧪Sport Science

The five health components are not independent — they affect each other. You cannot run a long distance (cardiovascular endurance) without leg muscles that resist fatigue (muscular endurance). Sport scientists also track skill-related components: speed, power, balance, coordination, agility, and reaction time. These are the bridge between general fitness and actual sport performance. Sprint speed and vertical jump are both expressions of power — strength applied quickly.

2
Lesson 2
Which Sports Train Which Components
Sport Top Components
SoccerCardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, speed, agility
GymnasticsFlexibility, muscular strength, balance, power
Football (offensive line)Muscular strength, power
Cross-country runningCardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance
BasketballAll five, with extra demand on cardio endurance and power
YogaFlexibility, muscular endurance, balance
3
Lesson 3
Your Personal Fitness Snapshot

You can test all five health-related components with simple at-home protocols. The goal is not to beat anyone else — it's to see your baseline so you can watch it move over a season.

  • Cardiovascular endurance — time yourself running a mile
  • Muscular strength — how many push-ups in a row, with good form?
  • Muscular endurance — how long can you hold a forearm plank?
  • Flexibility — sit-and-reach: how many inches past (or short of) your toes?
  • Body composition — measure waist and bicep circumference; watch them shift over months, not days
💡Did You Know?

Decathletes — track-and-field athletes who compete in 10 different events over 2 days — are sometimes called "the most all-around fit humans on the planet." They have to excel at events that demand opposite components, like shot put (pure power) and the 1500-meter run (pure endurance). They train all five health components plus all six skill-related ones year-round. Decathlon world champions are walking proof that total fitness is trainable.

4
Lesson 4
Training Components Together

The best workouts hit multiple components at once. Examples:

  • Obstacle course — strength (climbing), endurance (running), flexibility (crawling under)
  • Circuit training — alternates strength moves with cardio bursts
  • Sport scrimmage — natural blend of cardio, strength, and skill
  • Yoga flow — flexibility + muscular endurance + balance
🌎Real-World Connection

Physical therapists assess all five fitness components when athletes recover from injury. A torn ACL might regain strength quickly but lose flexibility — so the PT plans rehab to bring everything back into balance. The goal is never one big number; it's a balanced toolkit. The same logic applies to your training: don't just hit your favorite component. The weakest one is usually what limits the rest.

🔬Coach's Lab

Run the five-component fitness battery on yourself. One Saturday morning, test all five: mile run, max push-ups, max plank hold, sit-and-reach, waist measurement. Write all five numbers down with the date. In 6 weeks, run the same battery. Did all five improve, or only some? Which one barely moved? That's your weakest component — and that is exactly where the next training cycle should focus.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Fitness component — One of the five categories that make up total health-related fitness.
  • Cardiovascular endurance — How long heart and lungs can sustain activity.
  • Muscular strength — Maximum force a muscle can produce in one effort.
  • Muscular endurance — How long muscles can keep producing force.
  • Body composition — Ratio of muscle, fat, water, and bone in the body.
  • Power — Strength applied quickly — a skill-related component (stretch term).
  • Agility — The ability to change direction quickly without losing speed or balance (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Sara trains soccer 3×/week and does push-ups daily. She's been doing this for 2 months with no progress. Using the principle of progressive overload and the FITT framework, what should she change? Then: what is ONE measurement she should track to prove the change worked?

→What's Next

Next: complete the Fitness Component Writing assignment and Station challenge, then test your core in the Plank & Balance Flight Club.

Balance and Coordination: The Invisible Skills

Balance and coordination are the quiet skills behind every athletic move. You don't see them on a scoreboard, but the moment they fail you trip, drop, or get blocked. Athletes who look smooth almost always have well-trained balance and coordination — and sport scientists can measure exactly how much each contributes to performance. The good news is both can be trained at home with no equipment.

1
Lesson 1
Static vs. Dynamic Balance

Sport scientists divide balance into two types:

  • Static balance — holding a position without moving. Example: standing on one foot, eyes open.
  • Dynamic balance — keeping balance while moving. Example: running on a balance beam, dribbling a soccer ball at full speed.

Sports almost always need dynamic balance. But static balance is the foundation: if you can't hold a still position, you can't control a moving one. The center of gravity — the balance point of your body — is constantly shifting during movement, and your job is to track it.

🧪Sport Science

Balance comes from three sensory sources working together: the eyes (visual feedback), the inner ear (fluid-filled tubes that detect head motion and rotation), and proprioception — sensors in your joints and muscles that report position. When one source fails — like closing your eyes — the other two have to work harder. That's why one-foot standing is much harder with eyes shut. Sport scientists use this exact test to assess proprioception in athletes recovering from ankle injuries.

2
Lesson 2
What Coordination Means

Coordination is the smooth working-together of multiple body parts during movement. There are several specific types, and each one shows up in different sports:

👁️
Hand-Eye
Eyes tracking while hands perform — catching, throwing, hitting.
👣
Foot-Eye
Same idea, but with feet — soccer dribbling, jumping over obstacles.
👐
Bilateral
Both sides of the body working together — swimming strokes, jumping rope.
🔄
Cross-Lateral
Opposite arm and leg coordinating — walking, running, freestyle swimming.
3
Lesson 3
Why Athletes Train These Deliberately

A goalkeeper with bad hand-eye doesn't catch shots. A soccer player with weak foot-eye trips over the ball. A swimmer with poor bilateral coordination has an uneven stroke. Sport scientists call balance and coordination the skill-related fitness components — and they distinguish them from the five health-related components because they directly translate to sport performance.

💡Did You Know?

Babies don't have coordination at birth — they develop it month by month. First they learn to track an object visually (about 3 months). Then to reach for it (about 5 months). Then to bring their hands together (about 6 months). By age 1, they can pick something up with intent. The same building-block process happens when you learn a new sport skill, just faster — your brain builds the same kind of motor pathways, layer by layer.

4
Try It
Balance and Coordination Drills
🦩
One-Foot Stand
Hold 30 sec, then try with eyes closed. Switch feet.
🚶
Heel-to-Toe Walk
Walk a straight line, heel touching toe. 20 steps.
🦵
Stork Stand
Stand on one foot, opposite foot resting on the knee. Hold 30 sec each side.
🤹
Ball Toss
Toss a ball up, catch with both hands. Then ONE hand. Then add a clap.
🦘
Hop-Stick
Hop forward on one foot — stick the landing without wobbling. Try with eyes closed.
🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic figure skaters land jumps from heights of 2+ feet onto a quarter-inch metal blade — and they have to stick the landing while spinning, all while making it look smooth. That is dynamic balance, body awareness, and coordination working at the highest level humans have ever achieved. They got there by training the same fundamentals listed above, plus thousands of harder progressions, for a decade or more.

🔬Coach's Lab

Test the role of vision in your balance. Stand on one foot with eyes open. Time how long you can hold without wobbling or putting the other foot down. Rest. Now do the same test with eyes closed. Time both. Subtract: the difference is your vision dependency. Most untrained people hold for 30+ seconds eyes open but under 10 with eyes closed. Train one-foot stands with eyes closed for 4 weeks, retest, and watch the gap shrink.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Balance — The ability to control body position.
  • Static balance — Holding a still position without falling.
  • Dynamic balance — Keeping balance while moving.
  • Coordination — Smooth, organized movement of multiple body parts.
  • Hand-eye coordination — Eyes and hands working together accurately.
  • Proprioception — Your body's internal sense of where its parts are (stretch term).
  • Center of gravity — The balance point of the body during movement (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Time your one-foot stand on the right foot (eyes open). Then the left. Then both again with eyes closed. Write all four numbers. Which side is weaker? What's your eyes-open vs. eyes-closed gap? Practice for 4 sessions (5 minutes each). Retest. Did any of the four numbers improve? Use the data to identify your weakest combination.

→What's Next

Next: build your Skill-Related Fitness Profile, then test your core and control in the Plank & Balance Challenge.

pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.11 · Rhythmic Movement and Dance
Week 23

Rhythmic Movement and Dance: Training the Timing System

Dance and rhythmic movement are not just performance — they are some of the most powerful full-body training a sport scientist can prescribe. They develop coordination, timing, and kinesthetic awareness in ways that no straight-ahead training can match. Professional athletes from Steph Curry to Serena Williams have used dance and footwork-to-music training to sharpen the timing systems their sport requires.

1
Lesson 1
What Rhythmic Movement Means

Rhythmic movement is moving the body to a steady external beat or pattern. It sounds simple, but it requires the brain to do three things in tight sequence:

  • Hear or feel the beat
  • Predict when the next beat will arrive
  • Tell the muscles to fire on that beat — not before, not after

That timing skill is harder than it looks, which is why elite athletes train it on purpose. It's also why some people who are strong and fast still look "stiff" — their timing system isn't tuned.

2
Lesson 2
Why Dance Helps Athletes

Dance training improves several specific abilities that show up in nearly every sport:

🦶
Footwork
Quick, precise foot positions — foundation of boxing, tennis, defensive basketball.
⚖️
Balance
Holding positions on one foot and switching weight smoothly.
⏱️
Timing
Coordinating movement with external signals — the beat, an opponent, a ball.
🧠
Sequence Memory
Remembering and chaining movement sequences — useful for plays and routines.
🕺
Body Control
Knowing exactly where every limb is at any moment.
🧪Sport Science

Many NFL wide receivers take ballet classes during the off-season — yes, ballet. Ballet is the most demanding training in existence for footwork, balance, and body control. Players who add ballet measurably improve their agility scores and route-running precision. Boxers similarly use jump rope and footwork drills set to music. The external beat trains the body to move with timing under pressure — a skill that transfers directly to every fast-moving sport.

3
Lesson 3
Tempo, Beat, and Pattern

Music has a measurable structure you can move to:

  • Beat — the steady pulse you naturally tap to
  • Tempo — how fast the beat goes, measured in beats per minute (BPM)
  • Pattern — how beats group together, usually in sets of 4

If you can hear those three things, you can dance to anything. The rest is style. Sport scientists use the same three concepts when they program plyometric jump training — they pick a specific tempo for the jumps because the body adapts differently to slow vs. fast cadence.

💡Did You Know?

Humans are one of the few species — alongside parrots and a few other birds — that can synchronize movement with an external rhythm. Scientists call this beat induction. Other primates, including chimpanzees, generally cannot do it. Researchers think beat induction is wired into the same brain regions we use for language. So when you dance with friends, you're using one of the most uniquely human cognitive skills that exists in nature.

4
Lesson 4
Movement as Stress Management

Rhythmic movement isn't only physical training — it's one of the most effective tools sport scientists know for managing stress. When you move to a beat, your body lowers cortisol (the stress hormone) and releases endorphins, the brain chemicals that lift mood. That's why athletes use movement to reset mentally, not just to get fit.

A variety of fitness and wellness activities promote stress management — and dance is one of the strongest:

  • Rhythmic activities — dance, jump rope, and drumming pair movement with a beat, which research links to lower anxiety.
  • Yoga and stretching — slow movement paired with breathing calms the nervous system.
  • Steady aerobic activity — a walk, jog, or bike ride clears the head and improves sleep.
  • Gymnastics and skill practice — focused, absorbing movement crowds out worry, producing what scientists call a "flow" state.

The takeaway: when stress is high, the right move is often literally to move. Pick a rhythmic or wellness activity, give it 10–15 minutes, and measure the change in how you feel.

🌎Real-World Connection

Many pro and college teams now employ sport psychologists who prescribe movement and breathing routines for stress, not just strength coaches for muscle. Before high-pressure events, athletes use rhythmic warm-ups and music on purpose — the steady beat regulates heart rate and focus. Managing stress is treated as a trainable performance skill, the same as speed or strength.

5
Try It
Simple Rhythm Drills
👏
Clap Pattern
Play a song. Clap on every beat for 30 seconds. Then clap only on beats 1 and 3.
🏀
Dribble to a Beat
Bounce a ball on each beat of a song. Try faster tempos as it gets easier.
🦶
Footwork Box
Step front, side, back, side — one move per beat. Easy at slow tempo, hard at fast.
🕺
Mirror Move
With a partner, take turns copying each other's moves to the beat.
🌎Real-World Connection

Competitive cheer, marching bands, drill teams, and color guards combine high-level athleticism with rhythmic movement and team coordination. Cheer in particular has been recognized by sport scientists as one of the most physically demanding sports — combining gymnastics-level strength and flexibility with split-second team timing. The next time someone tells you dance isn't a sport, point them to a competitive cheer routine.

🔬Coach's Lab

Test how tempo affects your performance. Pick a simple move — jumping jacks, alternating foot taps, or boxing-style jab-jab. Do 30 seconds slow (about 60 BPM, one beat per second). Rest. Do 30 seconds at a moderate tempo (about 100 BPM). Rest. Do 30 seconds fast (about 140 BPM). Count clean reps at each tempo. At which tempo did your form break down? That's your timing edge — the rhythm at which the skill is no longer automatic.

6
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Rhythmic movement — Moving your body to a steady external beat or pattern.
  • Beat — The steady pulse that drives a rhythm.
  • Tempo — Speed of the beat, often measured in beats per minute.
  • Coordination — Smooth working-together of body parts during movement.
  • Timing — Acting at the right moment — neither early nor late.
  • Kinesthetic awareness — Your sense of where your body is in space (stretch term).
  • Beat induction — The brain's ability to synchronize movement with an external rhythm (stretch term).
  • Stress management — Using tools — including rhythmic movement, dance, yoga, and aerobic activity — to lower stress and reset mentally.
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Pick a tempo you can measure (a song's BPM, or use a free metronome app). Try a footwork box at 80 BPM for 30 seconds, then at 120 BPM. Count clean reps at each tempo. What was your "clean rep" ratio at each speed? Where did your form first break down — feet, balance, or timing? Use the data to identify your timing limiter.

→What's Next

Next: reflect on your dance experience and put rhythm in motion, then take the Flight Club Wall Sit Countdown.

pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.13 · Goal Setting and Personal Fitness Plans
Week 25

Goal Setting and Personal Fitness Plans: Train Like a Sport Scientist

Up to now you've studied what fitness is. Now you'll learn how to design your own training. Elite athletes don't just "work out" — they set specific, measurable goals, design plans built on FITT and progressive overload, track data, and adjust based on what the data shows. By the end of this unit you'll have your own personal fitness plan, built by you, for you, using the same framework Olympic coaches use.

1
Lesson 1
Why Goal Setting Works

Goal setting is not magic — it's measurable psychology. When you write down a clear goal, three things change in your brain:

  • You pay more attention to information related to the goal
  • You make better decisions when facing tradeoffs ("practice or watch TV?")
  • You can measure progress, which sustains motivation through hard stretches

Studies consistently show people who write down their goals are 2–3 times more likely to achieve them than those who only think about them. Writing forces specificity. Specificity makes progress measurable. Measurable progress sustains effort.

2
Lesson 2
SMART Goals

The most widely used goal-setting framework is SMART. Every letter is non-optional — drop one and the goal weakens.

🎯
Specific
Clear and detailed. Not "get fit" but "do 20 push-ups in a row."
📏
Measurable
Countable or measurable progress. Reps, time, distance.
✅
Achievable
Challenging but possible from your current baseline.
🎢
Relevant
Connected to a sport, hobby, or value that matters to YOU.
⏰
Time-bound
Has a deadline. "By April 30" beats "someday."

Example: "I will run a mile in under 9 minutes by April 30, by jogging 20 minutes three times a week and tracking my time every Sunday."

🧪Sport Science

Olympic athletes work with sport psychologists who help them set process goals (things you control day-to-day, like "stretch 10 minutes daily") AND outcome goals (results, like "win a gold medal"). The applied trick: focus daily attention on process goals. Outcomes follow process. If you focus only on the outcome, you tend to skip the steps that actually produce it. This is one of the most reliable findings in the entire field of sport psychology.

3
Lesson 3
Building a Personal Fitness Plan

A complete personal fitness plan has five parts. Each one is a layer of the FITT principle applied to your goal:

  1. Goal — written in SMART format
  2. Components to train — which of the 5 fitness components matter most for this goal?
  3. Weekly schedule — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type (FITT) for each session
  4. Progress checks — when and how will you re-measure?
  5. Adjustments — what will you change if data shows no progress?

One important rule: a plan you actually follow beats a perfect plan you abandon. Build something realistic, then progressively overload it.

💡Did You Know?

NFL teams plan their seasons using something called periodization — alternating phases of building strength, building speed, building endurance, and recovering. Elite athletes don't try to be at peak fitness all year round. They peak for the games that matter, then drop back into rebuild phases. Your fitness plan should follow the same logic: hard weeks AND recovery weeks. Recovery is part of the plan, not the absence of one.

4
Lesson 4
Tracking and Adjusting

The fanciest goal in the world fails without tracking. Athletes use:

  • A simple log — date, activity, duration, effort level, how it felt
  • Periodic re-tests — measure the goal metric every 2 weeks
  • Feedback partners — coach, family member, or friend who reviews with you

Don't be afraid to adjust. If progress is faster than expected, raise the goal. If progress is slower, change the plan, not the goal. A coach who never adjusts is a coach who never improves athletes.

🌎Real-World Connection

The strongest athletes — and most successful adults — share one habit: regular self-review. Olympians keep training journals. Surgeons review every case. Software engineers run "code reviews." All of them ask the same questions you should ask: What worked? What didn't? What will I do differently next time? This is called metacognition — thinking about your own thinking. Sport scientists rank it among the most powerful tools in skill acquisition.

5
Lesson 5
Using Technology to Assess, Design, and Evaluate Your Plan

A sport scientist uses tools to make training measurable — and you already carry most of them. Technology helps at all three stages of a fitness plan: assess where you're starting, design the plan, and evaluate whether it worked.

⌚
Wearables & phone sensors
Fitness watches and phone apps count steps, estimate heart-rate zones, and track workout time — data you would otherwise have to guess.
📊
Spreadsheets & log apps
A free spreadsheet or notes app turns your training log into a chart, so a trend — improving, flat, or declining — becomes visible.
🎥
Video
Filming a rep lets you analyze your form frame by frame — the same tool professional coaches use.
⏱️
Timers & metronomes
Free apps standardize your test conditions so a re-test is a fair comparison.

Match the tool to the stage:

  • Assess — use a stopwatch app to time your baseline mile, or a heart-rate app to find your resting and working heart rate.
  • Design — use a spreadsheet or planner app to lay out your weekly FITT plan so Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type are all written down.
  • Evaluate — graph your re-test numbers against your baseline; the chart tells you, with evidence, whether the plan worked.

The rule a sport scientist follows: the tool should produce a number you can compare over time. If it doesn't give you data, it's a gadget, not a training tool.

💡Did You Know?

Professional teams employ entire sports analytics departments. NBA arenas use camera systems that track every player's position about 25 times per second; soccer clubs fit players with GPS vests that measure distance, sprint speed, and workload to prevent injury. The same idea scales down to your phone — the team with the better data, used well, usually makes the better decisions. You don't need expensive gear; you need to actually look at the numbers you already collect.

🔬Coach's Lab

Build and run a 2-week mini-plan — with technology. Pick one specific, measurable goal (push-ups, plank time, mile pace, sit-and-reach inches). (1) ASSESS: use a timer or counting app to record your baseline number. (2) DESIGN: write your SMART goal and a 3-session-per-week FITT plan in a notes app or spreadsheet. (3) EVALUATE: log every session, then on day 14 re-test and chart your two numbers. Did the data prove progress? If yes, what worked? If not, which variable would you change next — F, I, T, or T — and why?

6
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Goal — An outcome you're working toward.
  • SMART — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound — the framework for goal setting.
  • Personal fitness plan — Your written plan for training toward a fitness goal.
  • Process goal — A goal about daily actions you control (stretch term).
  • Outcome goal — A goal about a result you want to achieve (stretch term).
  • Periodization — Planned phases of training that alternate hard work and recovery (stretch term).
  • Metacognition — Thinking about your own thinking — reviewing your progress (stretch term).
  • Sports technology — Tools — wearables, apps, video, spreadsheets — used to assess, design, and evaluate a fitness plan with real data.
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Write one SMART fitness goal for the next 30 days. Make it specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Now design the 30-day training plan using the FITT framework. Specify Frequency (days/week), Intensity (effort or load), Time (minutes/sets/reps), and Type (which exercises). Justify why each FITT variable fits your specific goal. Finally: what is the ONE measurement you'll check on day 31 to prove it worked?

→What's Next

Next: build your Personal Fitness Plan and create a fitness goal art project to lock it in for the rest of the year.

pages.title: Substances and the Athlete's Body
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.12 · Substance Use and Abuse Prevention
Week 27
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
HE.68.SUA.1.1HE.68.SUA.1.2HE.68.SUA.1.7HE.68.SUA.3.3

Substances and the Athlete's Body

You have spent this year learning to treat your body as a system you can measure and improve. Training is an input. Food is an input. Sleep is an input. Substances are inputs too — and they are the only category on that list that can undo a whole season of work in a single decision. This unit looks at alcohol, nicotine, marijuana, and prescription and illicit drugs the way a sport scientist looks at anything else: what does the evidence actually show?

1
Lesson 1
Deciding Before the Moment

Every substance decision you will ever face has the same shape. Someone offers. You have a few seconds. What you do in those seconds is not really about willpower — it is about whether you decided in advance.

Sport scientists call this pre-commitment, and elite athletes use it constantly. A distance runner decides on Sunday what Tuesday's workout will be, so Tuesday's tired brain does not get a vote. The same tool works here. A responsible decision runs through four checks:

  1. Name the actual choice. Not "do I want to fit in" but "do I want this substance in my body."
  2. Check the consequences — all of them. Health, legal, academic, athletic, and the effect on people who count on you.
  3. Check the perspectives of others. Who else is affected by this choice? A teammate, a driver, a younger sibling watching you?
  4. Decide in advance, and have the words ready. The refusal you have already practiced comes out in one second. The one you invent on the spot takes ten — and ten seconds is a long time under pressure.
🧪Sport Science

Your brain is not finished. The prefrontal cortex — the region you met in the sportsmanship unit, responsible for planning, judgment, and impulse control — is one of the last areas to fully develop, continuing into the mid-twenties. The reward system underneath it develops earlier. That gap is normal and temporary, but it means substances hit an adolescent brain differently than an adult one: the pull is stronger and the brakes are still being installed. This is exactly why starting young raises addiction risk, and why pre-committing to a decision works so well — it lets your planning brain answer while it is calm instead of while it is being rushed.

2
Lesson 2
Alcohol: The Terms and the Evidence

Alcohol is a depressant. That word does not mean it makes you sad — it means it slows down the central nervous system: reaction time, coordination, balance, judgment, and breathing. Every one of those is something you have spent this year training to improve.

Short-term effects of drinking include impaired judgment and coordination, slowed reaction time, slurred speech, nausea and vomiting, dehydration, memory gaps or blackouts, and — at high doses — alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency. Because alcohol impairs judgment first, the person drinking is the least reliable judge of how impaired they are.

Long-term effects of repeated use include damage to the liver, heart, and pancreas, disruption of the brain development happening right now, lasting problems with memory and learning, increased risk of several cancers, and the development of addiction.

There is also a specific athletic cost. Alcohol dehydrates you, interferes with the muscle protein synthesis you studied in Unit 1.3, disrupts the deep sleep where most recovery happens, and measurably slows reaction time into the following day. An athlete who drinks the night before is training a worse body the next morning.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Depressant — A substance that slows down the central nervous system, including reaction time, coordination, and breathing.
  • Binge drinking — Drinking a large amount in a short period, bringing blood alcohol to a dangerous level quickly.
  • Abstain / avoid — Choosing not to use a substance at all.
  • Intoxicated — Physically and mentally impaired by a substance.
  • Under the influence — Having enough of a substance in the body to affect judgment, coordination, or behavior.
  • Addiction — A disease in which a person keeps using a substance despite harm, because the brain has adapted to need it.
  • Alcoholism — Also called alcohol use disorder — addiction specifically to alcohol.
  • Sober / sobriety — Not under the influence of alcohol or other drugs.
  • Recovery — The ongoing process of healing and rebuilding a healthy life after addiction.
  • Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) — The measured amount of alcohol in the bloodstream — the number used by law and by medicine (stretch term).
3
Lesson 3
Nicotine, Tobacco and Vaping

Nicotine is a stimulant and it is highly addictive — more so for an adolescent brain than an adult one. Vaping devices deliver it in a form that is easy to hide and easy to use often, which is precisely what makes dependence form fast.

"It is just water vapor" is not accurate. The aerosol from a vape can carry nicotine, ultrafine particles that travel deep into the lungs, flavoring chemicals not designed to be inhaled, and metals from the heating coil. Health agencies have also documented serious vaping-associated lung injury, most strongly linked to THC-containing products containing vitamin E acetate.

For anyone who trains, the measurable cost is direct: reduced lung function, faster shortness of breath, and a lower ceiling on the VO2 max you studied in Unit 1.4. Nicotine also constricts blood vessels, which works directly against the oxygen-delivery system you have spent a year building.

4
Lesson 4
Marijuana and THC: Myth, Fact, and What "Everyone" Actually Does

Marijuana is the substance surrounded by the most confident-sounding claims, which makes it the best possible place to practice the fact versus fallacy test you learned in the nutrition unit: show me the evidence.

🧠
Myth: "It is natural, so it is safe."
Natural does not mean harmless — tobacco and poison ivy are natural too. Todays THC concentrations are far higher than those in products studied decades ago.
🔒
Myth: "You cannot get addicted."
Cannabis use disorder is a recognized medical condition, and the risk is substantially higher for people who begin using during adolescence.
👥
Myth: "Everyone is doing it."
National surveys consistently find that the large majority of middle schoolers have not used marijuana. Teens routinely overestimate how many peers use.
🎓
Myth: "It does not affect school or sport."
THC measurably impairs short-term memory, attention, reaction time, and coordination — the exact systems used for learning and for play.

The documented effects of THC on a developing brain include impaired short-term memory, reduced attention and ability to learn new material, slowed reaction time, and impaired coordination and judgment — which is also why driving under the influence of THC is dangerous and illegal. Research consistently associates regular adolescent use with poorer academic outcomes.

Consequences worth naming plainly: lower grades and lost learning time, removal from athletic eligibility under most school and league policies, legal consequences, damaged trust at home, money spent, and a measurable step away from goals you wrote down yourself in Unit 1.13.

🧪Sport Science

There is a well-studied effect called pluralistic ignorance: people systematically overestimate how common a behavior is among their peers, especially a risky one. Researchers measure it by asking students two questions — "what share of students your age use this?" and then measuring actual use. The estimate is almost always far higher than the reality. This matters because the belief itself drives behavior: students who think "everyone is doing it" are more likely to start. Correcting the perception is one of the few prevention strategies with consistent evidence behind it. So when someone tells you everyone is doing it, treat it exactly like a supplement ad — a claim with no study attached.

Teacher note (not student-facing guidance): Prevalence statements in this lesson are kept deliberately non-numeric so the page does not go stale. Before each school year, pair this lesson with the current-year Monitoring the Future survey (monitoringthefuture.org) or the Florida Youth Substance Abuse Survey (FYSAS) and have students compare their own class estimate against the published figure. That comparison is the assessed task in the Myth vs. Fact assignment.
5
Lesson 5
Prescription Drugs, Opioids and Fentanyl

A prescription drug is a medicine matched to one person, at one dose, for one condition, by a doctor who knows that person's history. Misuse is any use outside that: taking someone else's medicine, taking more than prescribed, taking it more often, or taking it to get high.

Opioids are a class of powerful pain medicines that includes oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, and fentanyl. Opioids slow breathing — that is the mechanism that makes an overdose deadly.

Fentanyl deserves its own paragraph. It is a synthetic opioid roughly fifty to one hundred times more potent than morphine, which means a quantity too small to see can be a lethal dose. It is now frequently pressed into counterfeit pills made to look exactly like real prescription medication, and it is mixed into other substances without the user knowing. This is the single most important fact in this unit: a pill that did not come from a pharmacy with your name on the label cannot be assumed to be what it appears to be.

Short- and long-term effects of prescription drug misuse include drowsiness and confusion, nausea, dangerously slowed breathing, tolerance requiring more of the drug for the same effect, physical dependence, addiction, and organ damage.

6
Lesson 6
Recognizing an Overdose — and Acting

You are not expected to be a paramedic. You are expected to recognize an emergency and get an adult and 911 fast. These are the signs of an opioid overdose:

😴
Cannot be woken
Unresponsive to a loud voice, a shake, or a hard knuckle rub on the breastbone.
🦼
Breathing slowed or stopped
Very slow, shallow, or absent breathing. Gurgling, choking, or snoring-like sounds.
🔵
Blue or gray lips
Lips, fingertips, or skin turning blue, gray, or ashen. Skin cold and clammy.
👀
Pinpoint pupils
Pupils shrunk to very small dots, even in dim light.

What to do: Call 911 immediately and say you think it is an overdose. Stay with the person. If naloxone (often called by the brand name Narcan) is available and an adult can administer it, it can reverse an opioid overdose. Keep the person on their side so they do not choke. Do not leave them alone, and do not assume they will "sleep it off."

Signs that someone may be misusing substances over time are different and slower: sudden drops in grades, losing interest in sport or activities they used to love, big changes in sleep or appetite, new secrecy, missing money or missing medicine from the house, and unexplained changes in mood or energy.

⚠️Safety & Support

Calling for help is the right call, every time. Florida's 911 Good Samaritan Act (section 893.21, Florida Statutes) exists specifically so that fear of getting in trouble does not stop someone from calling — it provides protection from certain drug-possession charges for a person who in good faith seeks medical help for someone experiencing an overdose. If you are ever unsure: call. No one has ever regretted calling 911 for a person who turned out to be fine.

🌎Real-World Connection

Professional and Olympic sport takes this seriously enough to build an entire testing infrastructure around it. Athletes at the elite level are subject to year-round testing, must declare every medication and supplement they take, and can lose titles and eligibility for substances they did not know were in a product. The principle underneath all of it is the one in this unit: you are responsible for what goes into your body, and "I did not know what was in it" is not a defense that protects your health or your career.

🔬Coach's Lab

Run a perceived-norms experiment. Before you look anything up, write down your own estimate: out of 100 students your age, how many do you think used marijuana in the past year? How many vaped? Write both numbers down and seal them. Now find the current published figure from a national survey such as Monitoring the Future, or the Florida Youth Substance Abuse Survey. Compare. How far off was your estimate, and in which direction? Then answer the sport-scientist question: if most people your age guess too high, what does believing the wrong number do to a person's decision-making in the moment?

🎯 Words to Know
  • Substance misuse — Using a substance in a way it was not intended or prescribed to be used.
  • Prescription drug — Medicine matched to one person, one dose, and one condition by a doctor.
  • Opioid — A class of powerful pain medicine that slows breathing; includes oxycodone, morphine, and fentanyl.
  • Fentanyl — A synthetic opioid many times more potent than morphine, often pressed into counterfeit pills (stretch term).
  • Overdose — Taking enough of a substance to cause a life-threatening reaction — with opioids, breathing slows or stops.
  • Naloxone (Narcan) — A medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose if given in time (stretch term).
  • Tolerance — Needing more of a substance to get the same effect (stretch term).
  • Pluralistic ignorance — Systematically overestimating how common a behavior is among peers (stretch term).
  • Pre-commitment — Deciding in advance what you will do, so the decision is not made under pressure (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Evidence prompt: Pick ONE claim from this reading that surprised you. State the claim, then explain what evidence supports it and why that evidence is stronger than a testimonial or something a friend told you. Finally, connect it to a specific goal you wrote in your Unit 1.13 fitness plan: how would using this substance change the data you would see on your day-30 retest? Be specific about the mechanism, not just the outcome.

→What's Next

Next: the rules and laws that apply, the refusal skills that actually work under pressure, and exactly where to get help — for yourself or for someone else.

Optima

Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.12 · Substance Use and Abuse Prevention
Week 28
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
HE.68.SUA.2.1HE.68.SUA.3.2HE.68.SUA.4.1HE.68.SUA.5.1HE.68.SUA.5.3HE.68.R.2.3HE.68.R.2.9

Rules, Laws, Refusal Skills and Getting Help

Knowing the science is half of it. The other half is knowing what the rules actually are, having words ready before you need them, and knowing exactly who to go to — for yourself or for someone else.

1
Lesson 1
Three Sets of Rules

Three different sets of rules apply to you at the same time, and they are not the same thing.

  • Family rules are set by the adults responsible for you. They can be stricter than the law, and they usually come with the most immediate consequences — and the most trust to rebuild.
  • School rules are set by your school and district. They typically cover possession and use on campus and at school events, and they usually carry athletic-eligibility consequences on top of disciplinary ones.
  • State laws are set by the Florida Legislature and apply everywhere in the state, regardless of what a family or school allows.

Rules and laws are not there to make life boring. Look at what every one of them is actually protecting: a brain that is still building itself, and other people on the road, on the field, and in the house.

2
Lesson 2
What Florida Law Says

Here is what Florida law says, in plain language. These are the ones that apply to people your age.

  • Alcohol. It is illegal in Florida for anyone under 21 to purchase or possess alcoholic beverages.
  • Driving — Zero Tolerance. Florida has a zero-tolerance law for drivers under 21: a blood alcohol level of 0.02 or higher (far below the adult 0.08 limit) results in an automatic driver license suspension. Practically speaking, that is close to any drinking at all.
  • Tobacco, nicotine and vapes. Florida law sets 21 as the minimum age to purchase tobacco and nicotine products, including e-cigarettes and vapes, and restricts possession by people under that age.
  • Marijuana and THC. Marijuana remains a controlled substance under Florida law. Florida permits medical use only for qualified patients with a physician certification and a state-issued card; there is no legal recreational use in Florida.
  • Getting help is protected. Under Florida's 911 Good Samaritan Act, a person who in good faith seeks medical assistance for someone experiencing an overdose is protected from certain drug-possession charges.
Teacher note (not student-facing guidance): Statute references for verification: alcohol possession under 21, s. 562.111, F.S.; driver under-21 zero tolerance, s. 322.2616, F.S.; tobacco and nicotine dispensing/possession age, ss. 569.101 and 877.112, F.S.; controlled substances, ch. 893, F.S.; medical use of marijuana, s. 381.986, F.S.; 911 Good Samaritan Act, s. 893.21, F.S. Statutes change — confirm current text at leg.state.fl.us before each school year, and pair this page with your district's current student code of conduct and athletic eligibility policy.
3
Lesson 3
Refusal Skills That Actually Work

A refusal skill is a skill. That means it follows the same rules as a jump shot or a warm-up: it is built through repetition before you need it, not invented in the moment. Athletes rehearse pressure situations on purpose. This is the same thing.

Six tools that work. Most people find one or two that fit how they actually talk — pick yours and practice saying them out loud.

🚫
The plain no
"No thanks, I am good." Short, no explanation offered. An explanation invites a negotiation.
🏃
The reason
"I have got a meet Saturday." True, specific, and hard to argue with.
🔁
The redirect
"Nah — hey, are we still going to the game after?" Answer, then move the conversation.
🚪
The exit
"I am going to head out." Leaving is always available and always allowed. You never owe anyone a debate.
📱
The code word
A pre-agreed text to a parent or guardian that means "come get me, no questions right now." Set this up before you need it.
👥
The ally
Decide with one friend in advance that you will back each other. Two people refusing is far easier than one.

Three things that make any of them stronger: say it early (the first offer is the easiest to refuse), say it once and then stop explaining, and use your body — a steady voice and eye contact read as settled, while a mumble reads as negotiable.

One specific scenario to decide about right now, because it is the one most likely to actually happen: you are offered a ride by someone who has been drinking or using. The answer is no, every time, no exceptions, and you call a trusted adult for a ride instead. Agree with your family in advance that this call will never get you in trouble.

💡Did You Know?

Negative peer pressure is rarely a dramatic dare. Researchers find it is usually much quieter — an assumption that you will join in, a joke at the expense of someone who says no, or simply everyone else doing something while nobody says anything. That is why the positive version is so powerful. In the sportsmanship unit you learned you tend to rise or fall to the standard of the people you train with. The most effective thing you can do about peer pressure is not just resist it. It is to become the person whose standard everyone else matches.

4
Lesson 4
Where to Get Help — For You or for Someone Else

Asking for help is not a confession. It is the same move as telling an athletic trainer your ankle hurts — early reporting is how small problems stay small.

🏫
At school
School counselor, school nurse, athletic director, or any teacher you trust. Counselors are trained for exactly this conversation.
🏠
At home
A parent, guardian, older sibling, or another trusted adult in your family.
📞
988
The Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Call or text 988, free and confidential, 24 hours a day.
🏥
SAMHSA Helpline
1-800-662-HELP (4357). Free, confidential, 24/7 treatment referral in English and Spanish. Also findtreatment.gov.
🚨
911
For any emergency — unresponsiveness, trouble breathing, suspected overdose. Call first, ask questions later.
🏚
In the community
Family doctor or pediatrician, county health department, and Florida Department of Children and Families substance abuse programs.

How to actually start the conversation. You do not need a speech. Any of these works: "Can I talk to you about something and not get in trouble for asking?" — "I am worried about a friend." — "I need help with something and I do not know who to ask."

And if it is about someone else: you are not betraying a friend by getting them help. The friend who gets an adult involved is the one who is actually acting like a teammate.

5
Lesson 5
Advocacy: Using Your Voice With Your Team

Advocacy means using your voice to help other people make a healthy choice. In sport, this is just leadership — the same skill you practiced in the teamwork unit, aimed at something that matters more than a scrimmage.

What effective peer advocacy actually looks like:

  • Correct the norm. When someone says "everyone does it," you have real data now. Say so.
  • Make refusing normal. If you say no first and easily, you have just made it far easier for the next person in the circle.
  • Back up the person who said no. One person refusing can be isolated. Two cannot.
  • Tie it to what people already want. Grades, playing time, a goal, a scholarship, a driver license. Advocacy lands better when it connects to something the listener already cares about.
  • Do it together. A campaign built by a group carries far more weight than one person lecturing.
🌎Real-World Connection

Peer-led prevention is not a school-assembly gimmick — it is a documented strategy. Programs where students design and deliver the message to other students consistently outperform programs where adults deliver the same message, because the source is credible in a way an adult cannot be. This is also why social-norms campaigns — the ones that simply publish the accurate number of students who do not use — are among the better-supported prevention approaches. You are the most persuasive messenger your classmates have.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Refusal skill — A practiced way of saying no clearly and quickly under social pressure.
  • Peer pressure — The influence peers have on your choices — positive when it raises your standard, negative when it lowers it.
  • Advocacy — Using your voice to help others make and keep a healthy choice.
  • Zero tolerance law — Florida law suspending the license of a driver under 21 with a BAC of 0.02 or higher.
  • Good Samaritan Act — Florida law protecting a person who seeks medical help in good faith for someone overdosing (stretch term).
  • Social norms campaign — A prevention approach that publishes accurate peer-behavior data to correct overestimates (stretch term).
  • Confidential — Information kept private, as in a conversation with a counselor or a helpline.
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Write down the refusal tool from Lesson 3 that best fits how you actually talk, and the exact words you would use. Then name the specific situation you are most likely to face in the next year. Rehearse your line out loud five times — genuinely, not in your head. Finally: identify the one adult you would call, and the one friend you would ask to be your ally. Having those two names decided in advance is the whole point of this lesson.

→What's Next

Next: put it to work. Five assignments and a class advocacy campaign — then Quiz 6 closes out the unit.
