Team Sports: Rules, Strategy and Equipment

You have spent this year building the parts — throwing, catching, kicking, striking, locomotion, teamwork. A team sport is where all of them get used at once, under pressure, against someone trying to stop you. This unit is the operating manual: the rules every team sport shares, the strategy underneath offense and defense, and the equipment that keeps you in the game.

1
Lesson 1
Every Team Sport Has the Same Skeleton

Team sports look wildly different — and underneath, they are built from the same six parts. Learn the skeleton once and you can pick up any new sport far faster.

  1. Objective. How you score, and what counts as a point.
  2. Playing area and boundaries. Where the game lives, and what happens when the ball leaves it.
  3. Number of players and positions. How many on the field, and who is responsible for what.
  4. Starting and restarting play. Tip-off, kickoff, serve, throw-in, free kick, inbound pass.
  5. Fouls and violations. What is illegal, and what the penalty is.
  6. Timing. Halves, quarters, sets, innings, or a target score.

This is a transfer skill — the same idea you met in Unit 1.9 when you saw that a pitch, a serve, and a kick all run on one kinetic chain. Sports rhyme.

🏀
Basketball
5 per side. Score by shooting through the hoop (2 or 3 points, 1 for a free throw). Dribble to move; travelling and double-dribble are violations. Fouls are contact that impedes an opponent. Restart with an inbound pass.
⚽
Soccer
11 per side (far fewer in modified play). Score in the goal. No hands except the goalkeeper inside the box. Restarts: throw-in, goal kick, corner kick, free kick. Offside prevents camping by the goal.
🏐
Volleyball
6 per side. Score by grounding the ball in bounds on the opponent side; rally scoring to 25, win by 2. Maximum three contacts per side, and no player may touch the ball twice in a row. Rotate on winning serve.
🏈
Flag Football
Usually 5-7 per side. Score by reaching the end zone (touchdown). Pulling the flag replaces the tackle. Offense gets a set number of downs to reach the next line to gain. No blocking below the waist; no flag guarding.
2
Lesson 2
Offensive Strategy: Making Space

Every offense in every invasion sport is trying to do the same thing: create space, then use it before it closes. Four principles do almost all the work.

  • Spread the defense. Players who bunch together are easy to guard — one defender covers two attackers. Width and depth force the defense to stretch, and stretching makes gaps.
  • Move the ball faster than a defender can run. A pass travels faster than legs. Two or three quick passes will beat a defense that a single dribbler cannot.
  • Support the player with the ball. The ball carrier needs at least two options — one ahead and one behind. A teammate standing still and watching is not an option.
  • Move without the ball. This is the one beginners skip and the one that decides games. Cutting, screening, and filling space drags defenders out of position and opens lanes for someone else.

Then there is transition: the seconds right after possession changes. The defense is disorganized and the space is at its biggest. The fastest-scoring moment in most sports is the first four seconds after a turnover.

3
Lesson 3
Defensive Strategy: Taking Space Away

Defense is the mirror image: shrink the space and delay the attack until help arrives. Start with the two systems.

  • Person-to-person. Each defender is responsible for one attacker. Clear accountability, and it travels with the attacker — but a mismatch or a screen can break it.
  • Zone. Each defender is responsible for an area. Strong at protecting the middle and cheap on energy — but it concedes space between zones, and the seams are exactly where a good offense passes.

Underneath either system, three jobs are always running at once:

  • Pressure — the closest defender denies the attacker time and an easy forward pass.
  • Cover — the second defender backs up the first, so being beaten is not fatal.
  • Balance — the remaining defenders protect the most dangerous space, usually the direct route to the goal or basket.

The single most common defensive error at this level is everyone chasing the ball at once. That empties the space behind, and the space behind is where the points come from.

🧪Sport Science

Coaches and analysts describe this with a simple idea: defend the dangerous space, not the ball. Tracking data from professional soccer and basketball shows that the highest-value defensive actions are usually not tackles or steals at all — they are positioning choices that make the dangerous pass unavailable, so the attack never happens. It is the Wayne Gretzky principle: elite performers read where the play is going, and get there first.

4
Lesson 4
Equipment and Safety, Sport by Sport

Safety procedures are general — check the space, warm up, hydrate, communicate. Equipment is specific. Knowing which gear a given sport requires, and checking it before you play, is part of the skill of that sport.

🏀
Basketball
Court shoes with grip and ankle support; mouthguard recommended. Check: dry floor, padded standards, correct inflation. Procedures: no jewelry, call for loose balls, clear the lane after a whistle.
⚽
Soccer
Shin guards (required in nearly all organized play), cleats matched to the surface, goalkeeper gloves. Check: goals anchored, field clear of debris, corner flags flexible.
🏐
Volleyball
Knee pads, court shoes; ankle braces if you have a history. Check: net height and tension, padded posts, no obstructions in the run-off area. Call the ball loudly to prevent collisions.
🏈
Flag Football
Mouthguard, flag belt worn correctly on the outside, cleats. Check: field free of holes and hazards. No jewelry. Two-hand-touch or flag-pull only — no tackling.
🚴
Cycling / skating
Properly fitted helmet is non-negotiable; wrist guards and pads for skating. Check: brakes, tire pressure, helmet strap snug and level.
⚾
Bat and racket sports
Batting helmet with faceguard, correct bat length and weight, eye protection for racquetball and squash. Check: grip tape, cracks, and a clear swing radius before you swing.
⚠️Safety & Support

Three rules that apply to every sport on this page. One: equipment that does not fit does not protect — a loose helmet or an oversized borrowed mouthguard is close to no equipment at all. Two: inspect before you play, not after something goes wrong. Three: report a hazard or a broken piece of gear immediately, even if it means stopping the game. Athletic trainers call this a two-minute cost that prevents a six-week injury.

🌎Real-World Connection

Officials are part of the rules, not opponents of them. In every organized league, the referee's job is to keep play safe and fair, and the rulebook exists so that a game between strangers can happen at all. That is also why the sportsmanship you practiced in Unit 1.10 is technically part of the rules — unsportsmanlike conduct is itself a foul in basketball, soccer, volleyball, and football. Respecting the official is not just manners; it is compliance with the sport.

🔬Coach's Lab

Chart the space. Watch five minutes of any team sport — live, recorded, or a game you play. Every time a team scores or nearly scores, pause and write down two things: (1) which offensive principle created the space (spread, quick passing, support, off-ball movement, or transition), and (2) which defensive job broke down (pressure, cover, or balance). Do this for five scoring chances. Which offensive principle showed up most? Which defensive job failed most? That pairing is the single most coachable pattern in the game you watched.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Objective — How a sport is scored and won.
  • Violation — A breach of a rule of play, usually returning possession to the other team.
  • Foul — Illegal contact or conduct, usually penalized with a free attempt or possession.
  • Offense — The team in possession, trying to score.
  • Defense — The team without possession, trying to prevent scoring and regain the ball.
  • Person-to-person defense — Each defender is responsible for one specific opponent.
  • Zone defense — Each defender is responsible for an area of the playing surface.
  • Transition — The moment possession changes, when space is largest and defenses are least organized (stretch term).
  • Off-ball movement — Moving purposefully without the ball to create space for yourself or a teammate (stretch term).
  • Modified game — A game with adjusted rules, team size, or space so more players get more touches.
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Take a team sport you know and modify it so that a group with very mixed skill levels all get real involvement. Change exactly three things — for example team size, field size, a required number of passes before scoring, or a rule that every player must touch the ball. For each change, predict what it does to the amount of space on the field and to the number of touches the least confident player gets. Which of your three changes would improve the game the most, and why?

→What's Next

Next: learn a rulebook, break down offense and defense in a real game, build a safety and equipment checklist, and then actually play modified small-sided games and log what happened.

Week 31
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)

Gymnastics, Tumbling and Apparatus

Gymnastics is where balance, strength, flexibility and coordination stop being separate components and become one continuous movement. Everything in this unit is built from four actions — traveling, rolling, balancing, and transferring weight — combined into sequences that flow.

1
Lesson 1
The Four Building Blocks

Every tumbling sequence, cheer routine, parkour line and floor exercise ever performed is assembled from four actions:

  • Traveling — moving from one place to another: the eight locomotor skills from Unit 1.7, plus crawling, sliding and rolling along the floor.
  • Rolling — the body rotating around one of its axes: log roll, egg roll, shoulder roll, forward roll.
  • Balancing — holding a still shape over a base of support: one foot, two hands and one foot, a shoulder stand, an arabesque.
  • Transfer of weight — moving your body mass from one base of support to another: feet to hands, hands to feet, foot to foot, feet to back.

A sequence is these actions chained so that the end of one becomes the start of the next. That is what makes a routine look smooth instead of like a list of tricks.

🧪Sport Science

The technical term for what makes a sequence flow is the base of support and where your center of gravity sits over it. You are balanced while your center of gravity stays above your base; you begin to travel the instant it moves outside. Skilled gymnasts do not fight this — they use it, deliberately letting the center of gravity fall past the base to start the next movement, then catching it with a new base. That is why a good routine looks like it is being pulled forward rather than pushed: every element is set up by controlled imbalance from the one before it.

2
Lesson 2
Stunts and Tumbling — Build in Order

Tumbling is trained in progressions. You earn the next skill by owning the one before it. Skipping steps is the single most common cause of injury in this unit.

🪨
Log roll
Lie straight, arms overhead, roll sideways along the mat keeping the body in one line. Teaches rotation and body tension.
🥚
Egg roll
Tuck into a ball, knees to chest, and roll sideways. Teaches a tight tuck — the shape every later roll needs.
🔄
Forward roll
Squat, hands down shoulder-width, chin tucked to chest, push with the legs and roll along the upper back — never the head or neck — and come up to a squat.
🧗
Shoulder roll
Roll diagonally across one shoulder instead of straight over the spine. The safer roll on hard surfaces; used in martial arts and parkour.
🥋
Tripod / tuck balance
Hands and head form a triangle on the mat, knees rest on the elbows. Builds the base and the shoulder strength for inverted work.
🤸
Cartwheel
A sideways transfer of weight: hand, hand, foot, foot, in a straight line. Start against a line on the floor; keep arms and legs long.
⚠️Safety & Support

Read this before you tumble. Work on a mat, grass, or carpet — never a hard or slippery floor. Clear a space at least two body lengths in every direction. Always tuck your chin to your chest in a forward roll so your weight lands on the upper back, never the head or neck. Do not attempt any inverted skill without an adult present. Take off jewellery, tie back long hair, and go barefoot or in grip socks rather than loose shoes. Master each progression before moving to the next — and if a skill is not working, go back one step rather than pushing through it. No handsprings, flips, or aerial skills in this unit; those require a coach and equipment you do not have at home.

3
Lesson 3
Balance: Shapes, Levels and Lines

A balance is a still shape you hold for at least three seconds. Three variables turn a handful of shapes into dozens:

  • Base of support — what is touching the floor. Two feet, one foot, one foot and one hand, two hands and a head, the shoulders, the seat.
  • Level — low (on the floor), medium (crouched or kneeling), or high (standing, on the toes, arms extended).
  • Shape — straight, tucked, straddled, piked, twisted, arched. Symmetrical shapes look stable and calm; asymmetrical shapes look dynamic.

Good sequences deliberately change level and shape. A routine performed entirely at standing height reads as flat, no matter how hard the individual skills are.

4
Lesson 4
Apparatus: Small and Large

Apparatus just means equipment you perform with or on. It changes what your body has to solve.

  • Small apparatus is handled: a hoop, a ball, a rope, a ribbon or scarf, a beanbag, a wand. It adds a manipulative demand on top of the movement — you now have to control an object and your body, which is exactly the dual-task cost that makes doing two things at once harder than either alone.
  • Large apparatus is travelled on or over: mats, a low bench or beam, a taped line on the floor, a sturdy step, a wall for support. It constrains where your base of support can be, which forces precision.

Safe substitutions at home: a taped line or a length of 2x4 flat on the ground for a beam, a folded blanket or rug for a mat, a skipping rope or scarf for ribbon, a stair step for a low platform. Never use furniture, railings, or anything unstable as apparatus.

5
Lesson 5
Making It Flow — and Making It Fit the Beat

Now put it together. A sequence is judged on the transitions as much as the elements. Four rules:

  1. End where the next skill starts. If a roll finishes in a squat, the next element should begin from a squat.
  2. Change level at least twice. Low to high to low reads as a routine; all-medium reads as a warm-up.
  3. Hold every balance for three full seconds. A balance that is passed through is not a balance.
  4. Finish on purpose. Stick a clear final shape and hold it. Sport scientists call this an intentional endpoint, and it is what separates a routine from stopping.

Add rhythm and you are doing what you studied in Unit 1.12: hearing the beat, predicting the next one, and firing the movement exactly on it. Working with a partner or group adds one more layer — now you are matching each other as well as the beat, which is the timing skill behind every cheer squad, drill team and synchronized routine.

🌎Real-World Connection

Competitive cheer, drill team, colour guard, artistic and rhythmic gymnastics, diving, figure skating and freestyle skiing all score the same underlying things: difficulty, execution, and artistry — how well the elements connect and match the music. Judges deduct for a wobble, a broken line, or a step out of a landing precisely because those are the visible evidence that the center of gravity got away from the base of support. The scoring sheet is applied biomechanics.

🔬Coach's Lab

Test level change against perceived difficulty. Build a short sequence of four elements that all happen at the same level. Perform it and time it. Now rebuild it with the same four elements but force a level change between each one. Time it again. Which version took longer? Which felt harder in your legs and core, and where specifically? Sport scientists would predict the level-changing version costs more energy because you are repeatedly raising and lowering your center of gravity against gravity. Did your body agree?

🎯 Words to Know
  • Sequence — Two or more movements linked so the end of one leads into the start of the next.
  • Base of support — The parts of the body touching the ground and the area between them.
  • Transfer of weight — Moving body mass from one base of support to another.
  • Apparatus — Equipment used in a routine — small (handled) or large (travelled on).
  • Static balance — Holding a still shape over a base of support.
  • Level — The height at which a movement happens — low, medium, or high.
  • Symmetry / asymmetry — Whether the two sides of a shape match; asymmetry reads as more dynamic (stretch term).
  • Progression — An ordered series of skills where each one prepares the body for the next (stretch term).
  • Intentional endpoint — A deliberate, held finishing shape that signals the routine is complete (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Pick one tumbling skill from Lesson 2 you cannot yet do cleanly. Work out which earlier progression it actually depends on, and which physical quality is the limiter — core strength, shoulder strength, flexibility, or confidence. Design a two-week FITT plan targeting that specific limiter, and name the measurement that would prove you were ready to try the full skill.

→What's Next

Next: design and perform your own tumbling sequence, build an apparatus routine to a beat with a partner or group, and create a rhythmic movement sequence together.

Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.14 · Outdoor Pursuits and Activity Opportunities
Week 33
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
PE.7.M.1.4PE.6.C.2.21PE.6.C.2.22PE.7.C.2.8PE.6.M.1.12

Outdoor Pursuits and Training in the Elements

Outdoor pursuits are the activities people keep doing for their whole lives — long after the school team ends. They are also the ones where the environment gets a vote. This unit covers the introductory skills, and the precautions that keep weather from turning a good session into an emergency.

1
Lesson 1
What Counts as an Outdoor Pursuit

An outdoor pursuit is a physical activity done in a natural or outdoor setting, usually self-paced, usually requiring some navigation, planning, or environmental judgment. They matter for a specific reason: participation in team sports drops sharply after high school, but people hike, cycle, paddle and climb into their seventies.

🥾
Hiking and trail walking
The most accessible outdoor pursuit there is. Skills: route selection, pacing, footwear, hydration planning, and trail etiquette.
🧭
Orienteering
Navigating a course using a map and compass. Skills: orienting the map, cardinal directions, pacing count, reading terrain features.
🚴
Cycling
Road, path, or trail. Skills: helmet fit, hand signals, scanning, gear selection, basic maintenance.
🗻
Paddling
Canoe, kayak, or paddleboard. Skills: PFD fit, basic strokes, launching. Always with supervision and a life jacket.
🧗
Climbing and bouldering
Indoor wall or supervised outdoor. Skills: three points of contact, footwork over arm strength, spotting and falling safely.
📍
Geocaching and trail running
GPS treasure hunting and off-road running. Skills: navigation, terrain reading, pacing on uneven ground.
2
Lesson 2
Introductory Skills: Navigate, Pace, Tread Lightly

Three skill sets carry across nearly every outdoor pursuit.

Navigation. Start with the four cardinal directions — north, east, south, west, clockwise from the top. To orient a map, turn the map (not yourself) until north on the map points to north on the ground. A compass needle always points to magnetic north. Then learn to read handrails (a long feature you can follow, like a stream, fence, or trail) and catching features (something you will obviously hit if you have gone too far, like a road or a ridge). Those two ideas prevent most of the ways people get lost.

Pacing. Count how many double-steps you take to cover 100 metres on flat ground — most middle schoolers land somewhere around 60–70. That is your pace count, and it lets you estimate distance without any equipment. Uphill it goes up; downhill it goes down. Outdoor pursuits are almost always Zone 2 work: a pace you could hold while talking, sustained for a long time. Going out too fast is the single most common beginner error.

Tread lightly. The Leave No Trace principles: plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly (pack out everything you pack in); leave what you find; minimize campfire impacts; respect wildlife; and be considerate of other visitors.

Trail etiquette has right-of-way rules, and they exist for safety: hikers going uphill have the right of way; cyclists yield to hikers; and everyone yields to horses. Announce yourself before passing someone from behind.

💡Did You Know?

The ten essentials is a checklist that mountaineers developed in the 1930s and that search-and-rescue teams still recommend today: navigation, sun protection, insulation (extra layers), illumination (headlamp), first-aid supplies, fire, repair kit and tools, extra food, extra water, and emergency shelter. The reasoning is not that you expect to need all ten — it is that the cost of carrying them is small and the cost of needing one and not having it can be enormous. It is the same risk logic as the warm-up.

3
Lesson 3
Precautions in Extreme Weather and Environmental Conditions

Weather is a training variable. A sport scientist checks it the same way they check a heart-rate zone — before the session, not during it.

🌡
Heat
Hydrate before you feel thirsty. Train early or late, not midday. Light-coloured, loose, breathable clothing. Build up over 10-14 days. Take shaded breaks. Watch for the heat illness ladder: cramps, exhaustion, stroke.
💧
Humidity
High humidity blocks evaporative cooling, so sweat stops working. The heat index can be far higher than the air temperature. Cut intensity and duration, and add breaks, when humidity is high.
❄
Cold
Layer: a wicking base, an insulating middle, a wind or water resistant shell. Avoid cotton next to skin. Cover head, hands and ears. Watch for hypothermia (shivering, confusion, slurred speech) and frostbite (numb, waxy, white skin). Wind chill makes it far colder than the thermometer says.
⚡
Lightning
When thunder roars, go indoors. Use the 30-30 rule: if thunder follows the flash within 30 seconds, seek shelter immediately, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before returning. Lightning is Floridas single most relevant outdoor hazard.
☀
Sun and UV
Check the UV index. Broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every two hours and after sweating or swimming. Hat and sunglasses. UV is strongest roughly 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and it penetrates cloud.
🌪
Air quality and wind
Check the Air Quality Index. Above 100, people with asthma should reduce exertion; above 150, everyone should shorten intense outdoor work. Wildfire smoke and high ozone both matter. Strong wind adds chill and makes paddling and cycling hazardous.
⚠️Safety & Support

Florida-specific: this state leads the nation in lightning strikes, and the combination of high heat with high humidity is the dangerous one — humidity is what stops sweat from cooling you. Check the heat index rather than the temperature alone, build heat acclimatization gradually over one to two weeks, and treat any thunder at all as a full stop. Recognizing the heat illness ladder you learned in Unit 1.6 — cramps, then exhaustion, then stroke — is a required outdoor skill here, not an optional one.

🌎Real-World Connection

Every serious outdoor program in the country runs on the same decision tool: a go / no-go check made before departure. Guides, camps and school programs check the forecast, the heat index, the lightning risk, the air quality, and the group's readiness — and they cancel. The professional skill is not toughness; it is being willing to call it off. Search-and-rescue data consistently shows that most incidents trace back to a decision made before anyone left the trailhead.

🔬Coach's Lab

Build and test a pace count. Measure 100 metres (about 110 large steps, or use a phone GPS or a track straightaway). Walk it at a steady pace, counting only every time your right foot lands. That number is your pace count. Repeat three times and average. Now test it: pick an unmeasured distance, predict it using your pace count, then check with a GPS app. How close were you, as a percentage? Then walk the same 100 metres uphill and count again. By how much did your pace count change, and why does that matter for estimating distance on real terrain?

🎯 Words to Know
  • Outdoor pursuit — A self-paced physical activity in a natural setting requiring planning or navigation.
  • Orienteering — Navigating a course using a map and compass.
  • Cardinal directions — North, east, south and west.
  • Pace count — The number of double-steps you take to cover a set distance, used to estimate distance.
  • Leave No Trace — Seven principles for minimizing your impact on an outdoor space.
  • Heat index — How hot it actually feels when humidity is combined with air temperature (stretch term).
  • Wind chill — How cold it actually feels when wind is combined with air temperature (stretch term).
  • Hypothermia — Dangerously low body temperature — shivering, confusion, slurred speech (stretch term).
  • Frostbite — Freezing of skin and tissue, most often on fingers, toes, ears and nose (stretch term).
  • Air Quality Index (AQI) — A scale reporting how polluted the air is and who should limit outdoor exertion (stretch term).
  • 30-30 rule — Shelter if thunder comes within 30 seconds of a flash; wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
📝Weekly Reflection

Planning prompt: Choose one outdoor pursuit and one Florida month. Look up the typical conditions for that month — temperature, humidity, storm pattern, UV index. Write the go / no-go criteria you would set in advance: what specific reading on which measurement would make you cancel, shorten, or reschedule? Explain why deciding those thresholds beforehand is more reliable than deciding in the moment.

Where to Move: School, Community and Beyond

Everything you have learned this year is worth exactly as much as you actually use it. This lesson is about finding the door — the real, specific places where a person your age can go be active in fitness, wellness, gymnastics and dance.

1
Lesson 1
In-School Opportunities

Schools offer far more than the PE period, and most of it is free and already paid for.

🏅
Interscholastic teams
School teams that compete against other schools. Tryouts, a season, and a coach. The most structured option.
🥎
Intramurals
Leagues and clubs that play within your own school. Usually no tryout and no cut - the easiest door to walk through.
💃
Dance and gymnastics clubs
Dance team, cheer, tumbling club, step team, colour guard. These cover the gymnastics and dance activities in Unit 1.16.
🏃
Before and after school
Running club, walking club, weight room hours, open gym, morning fitness, esports-plus-fitness programs.
🧘
Wellness programs
Yoga or mindfulness clubs, stress-management groups, health clubs, and school wellness challenges.
🏆
Events
Field day, fun runs, fitness challenges, intramural tournaments, and school-wide step competitions.
💡Did You Know?

Intramural programs exist specifically for the students who are not on a varsity team — which is most students. Research on youth activity consistently finds that the biggest barrier is not motivation or ability but not knowing what is available and assuming you are not good enough. That second half is the important one: intramurals are designed with no cut precisely so that assumption is wrong. The people who run them are usually delighted when someone new asks.

2
Lesson 2
Community Opportunities

Outside school, most communities have far more than people realize, at a wide range of costs.

🏟
Parks and Recreation
City and county rec departments run youth leagues, swim lessons, tennis, open courts and fields. Usually the lowest-cost organized option, and often with fee waivers.
🏊
Community centres and YMCA
Pools, gyms, group fitness, youth programs. Many offer sliding-scale or financial-assistance memberships.
🤾
Clubs and studios
Gymnastics gyms, dance studios, martial arts dojos, climbing gyms, swim clubs, cycling clubs. Most offer a free or cheap trial class.
🌴
Trails, parks and greenways
Free, open, and everywhere. Walking and cycling trails, state parks, boardwalks, beaches, disc golf courses, outdoor fitness stations.
⛪
Faith and neighbourhood groups
Church, temple and neighbourhood leagues, scouting, 4-H, Boys and Girls Clubs - often free and close to home.
📱
Online and at home
Free guided workout, yoga and dance videos; running and cycling apps; VR fitness. Zero cost, zero travel, on your schedule.
3
Lesson 3
How to Find It — and How to Judge Whether It Fits

Where to look: your school's activities or athletics page and morning announcements, the school counsellor or athletic director, your city or county Parks and Recreation website, the public library's community board, and simple searches like "youth [activity] near [your city]".

The five questions to ask before you commit — this is the part most people skip:

  1. Cost. What is the real total — fees, equipment, uniform? Is there a scholarship, fee waiver, or sliding scale? Ask; they almost always exist and are almost never advertised.
  2. Transport. Can you actually get there and back, reliably, every session?
  3. Time. How many days a week, and does that fit around school and sleep?
  4. Level. Is it for beginners? Is there a cut? Is there a recreational division as well as a competitive one?
  5. Fit. Does it train something you actually enjoy, and does it target a fitness component you want to improve?

That last one is the sport-science question. In Unit 1.13 you identified your weakest component. The best opportunity for you is usually the one that is genuinely fun and happens to train that weakness — because the plan you follow beats the perfect plan you quit.

🌎Real-World Connection

Participation in organized youth sport drops sharply through the teen years, and the reasons young people give in survey after survey are remarkably consistent: it stopped being fun, there was too much pressure, or they did not feel good enough. Notice that none of those is "I stopped liking movement." This is exactly why knowing the full range of options matters — someone who leaves a competitive team and believes that was the only door often stops moving altogether, while someone who knows about intramurals, a trail, a climbing gym or a dance studio simply changes doors and keeps going for the next sixty years.

🔬Coach's Lab

Audit your own access. Draw three circles: things within walking distance of home, things within a short ride, and things at school. Place every activity opportunity you can find into a circle. Now count. Which circle has the most, and which of the five fit questions is your real limiter — cost, transport, time, level, or fit? Then find one specific opportunity you did not know existed before this assignment. That single discovery is the point of the exercise.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Intramural — A league or club that competes within a single school, usually with no tryout or cut.
  • Interscholastic — A school team that competes against other schools.
  • Parks and Recreation — The city or county department that runs public youth leagues, pools and facilities.
  • Sliding scale — A fee that adjusts to what a family can afford (stretch term).
  • Fee waiver — A reduction or removal of a program cost for families who qualify (stretch term).
  • Greenway — A public path or trail corridor for walking and cycling (stretch term).
  • Barrier to participation — Anything that stops someone taking part - cost, transport, time, skill level, or confidence.
📝Weekly Reflection

Action prompt: Name one in-school opportunity and one community opportunity you would genuinely consider. For each, answer all five fit questions honestly. Then identify the single biggest barrier standing between you and actually showing up — and write one concrete step you could take in the next two weeks to remove it. Not a plan for someday: a step with a date on it.

Games From Around the World

Every culture on earth invented ways to play, and they did not all invent the same ones. The games below come from six different parts of the world — and each one trains something the others do not. Playing someone else's game is one of the fastest ways to find a gap in your own movement vocabulary.

1
Lesson 1
Why Cultures Build Different Games

Games are shaped by what a place has. Open grassland tends to produce running and throwing games. Dense forest and villages produce games in tight spaces. Coastal cultures produce swimming, paddling, and games played on sand. Long winters produce games on ice and snow. Limited equipment produces games built around a single ball, a stick, or nothing at all.

That is why playing games from other cultures is genuinely useful training and not just a novelty: a game invented under different constraints will demand a skill combination your own sports never asked for. A player raised on basketball has excellent hand-eye coordination and almost no experience striking a ball with the sole of the foot. Sepak takraw fixes that in ten minutes.

🧪Sport Science

Movement scientists describe this as expanding your motor vocabulary. Every distinct movement pattern you learn builds a new neural pathway, and pathways are reusable — a skill learned in one activity transfers to any other activity that shares its mechanics, which is exactly benchmark PE.7.C.2.9 in action. Athletes who played many varied sports and games as children consistently show better general coordination and adaptability than those who specialized early in one. Sport scientists call it sampling, and the research on early specialization keeps pointing the same direction: variety early, specialization later.

2
Lesson 2
Six Games, Six Continents

Each of these can be adapted to a driveway, a yard, or a gym. Approach each one as something to learn, not a curiosity — these are real sports with real histories and, in several cases, professional leagues and national teams.

🇵
Tinikling - Philippines
A traditional folk dance in which dancers step in and out between two bamboo poles tapped on the beat. Trains timing, footwork and rhythm. Safe version: two jump ropes or broomsticks slid along the floor, slow tempo first.
🇮
Kabaddi - South Asia
A raider crosses into the opposing half chanting kabaddi on one breath, tries to tag defenders, and must return before breathing. Trains agility, breath control and anticipation. Safe version: no-contact tag-only rules.
🇹
Sepak Takraw - Southeast Asia
Volleyball where only feet, knees, chest and head may touch the ball. Trains foot-eye coordination and flexibility. Safe version: balloon or soft ball, lowered net or a rope, no acrobatic kicks.
🇮
Bocce / Petanque - Italy and France
Roll or toss balls as close as possible to a small target ball. Trains precision, touch and tactical thinking. Safe version: any set of balls plus a small marker, on grass or a driveway.
🇧
Capoeira - Brazil
Developed by enslaved Africans in Brazil, blending martial arts, dance and music, played in a circle called a roda. Trains balance, core strength and flow. Safe version: learn the ginga basic step and two simple movements only, no partner contact.
🇨
Jianzi - China
Keep a weighted shuttlecock in the air using feet, knees and heels - a two-thousand-year-old game still played in parks daily. Trains foot-eye coordination and balance. Safe version: a footbag, a rolled sock, or a balloon.
🌎Real-World Connection

Several games in this list are far bigger than most Americans realize. Kabaddi has professional leagues broadcast to tens of millions of viewers across South Asia. Sepak takraw is a medal sport at the Asian Games. Netball is played by millions across the Commonwealth, mostly by women, and has full professional leagues. And lacrosse — a mainstream American college sport — originated with Haudenosaunee and other Indigenous nations of North America, who played it for centuries before European contact and still field a national team today. The map of world sport is much larger than any one country's television schedule.

3
Lesson 3
Playing Someone Else's Game Respectfully

These games belong to living cultures, and some of them carry real historical weight — capoeira was developed under slavery, and lacrosse holds spiritual significance for the nations that created it. Four ground rules:

  • Learn where it comes from before you play it. The origin is part of the game.
  • Use the real name and pronounce it as well as you can. Look it up.
  • Do not treat it as a costume or a joke. Play the game; do not perform a stereotype of the people who invented it.
  • Notice what it is good at. Every one of these games survived for a reason — find the skill it builds better than anything you already play.
🔬Coach's Lab

Find your gap. Pick the game on this page that uses the skill you have practised least this year — for most students that is a foot-based game like sepak takraw or jianzi. Play it for ten minutes and count your successful reps in the first two minutes and in the last two minutes. Did the number improve inside a single session? A fast improvement usually means you had the underlying athleticism and were simply missing the specific pattern — which is exactly what motor vocabulary means. Now name the sport you already play that this new skill would transfer into.

🎯 Words to Know
  • Motor vocabulary — The full set of movement patterns a person has learned and can call on.
  • Sampling — Playing many varied sports and games early rather than specializing in one (stretch term).
  • Adaptation of rules — Changing a game so more people, at more ability levels, can take part safely.
  • Foot-eye coordination — Eyes and feet working together accurately - the core skill of several games on this page.
  • Traditional game — A game passed down within a culture, often long before organized modern sport.
📝Weekly Reflection

Comparison prompt: Choose one game from this page and one sport you already play. Identify one skill they genuinely share and one skill that is unique to the new game. Then answer the sport-scientist question: if you played the new game twice a week for a month, which fitness component or skill-related component would improve most, and what measurement would prove it?

→What's Next

Next: pick one, learn it properly, play it, and bring what you found back to the group.

Four scenarios. Read the person, weigh the perspectives, choose, and defend the choice.

1
Step 1
Respond With Empathy

For each scenario, write (a) what the person is most likely feeling, (b) what circumstances might be behind it that you cannot see, and (c) the exact words you would say, in quotation marks.

  1. A teammate misses the shot that would have won the game and walks off without speaking to anyone.
  2. A new student stands at the edge of the group during a warm-up and does not join in.
  3. A friend snaps at you for no reason during practice, which is not like them.
  4. A player on the other team is clearly upset after being called for a foul they say they did not commit.
2
Step 2
Practise Active Listening

Pick scenario 3. Write the conversation as a short back-and-forth script, at least six lines. Your lines must show active listening — letting them finish and reflecting back what you heard before you add anything of your own. Then mark the one line where you were most tempted to jump in with advice, and explain why you held off.

3
Step 3
Run the Four Lenses

Here is the decision: your team has figured out that an opponent's best player has an injured ankle, and a teammate suggests attacking that side all game.

Run it through all four lenses — Me, Them, The rules, Later — writing a real answer for each. Then state your decision and defend it.

4
Step 4
Generate Three Solutions

New problem: two players on your team have stopped speaking to each other and it is affecting how the whole team plays.

Generate three genuinely different solutions. For each, predict the outcome for the two players, for the rest of the team, and for you. Then choose one and explain why it produces the best outcome for the most people — not just the easiest outcome for you.

5
Step 5
Your Setback Plan

Name a real challenge that is most likely to derail your Unit 1.13 fitness plan in the next month. Then write your strategy using at least three of the six from the reading: time management, setting boundaries, realistic goals, self-care, scaling instead of skipping, or asking for support. Be concrete — what will you actually do, and when?

6
Step 6
Rules That Apply

Name one school rule and one community law that apply to something in your life right now. For each, explain who it protects and what would go wrong in a community if most people ignored it.

🚀 Flight Club Card Challenge

Random exercises drawn from a deck of cards. Sportsmanship in action — you don't choose what comes up, and you finish what you draw. Bonus: stretches first.

1
Warm Up — Reach for the Sky

How to Do It:

  • Stand up tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
  • Stretch both arms up as high as possible, reaching for the sky.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then relax.
  • Optional: Wiggle your fingers like you're grabbing stars!

Benefits: Stretches arms, shoulders, and back.

2
Warm Up — Hug Yourself

How to Do It:

  • Wrap your arms around yourself like you're giving a big hug.
  • Gently pull your shoulders forward while keeping your back straight.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then switch arm positions (whichever arm was on top, switch it).

Benefits: Stretches shoulders and upper back.

3
Materials Needed
  • Option 1: A real deck of playing cards
  • Option 2: Internet access and the Calculator Soup Random Card Generator
4
Draw a Card
  • If using a real deck, shuffle and draw one card at a time.
  • If using Calculator Soup, select 1 card, click Draw, and see your result.
5
Match the Card to the Exercise

Use the chart below to know which exercise to do. The number or face value tells you how many repetitions.

Suit Exercise Example
♥ HeartsJumping Jacks8♥ = 8 jumping jacks
♠ SpadesPush-UpsK♠ = 13 push-ups
♦ DiamondsSit-Ups/Crunches4♦ = 4 sit-ups
♣ ClubsSquatsJ♣ = 11 squats

Card Values

  • Ace = 14
  • King = 13
  • Queen = 12
  • Jack = 11
  • Numbers = Same as card value
6
Complete 10–20 Draws

Each time you draw a card, complete the exercise before drawing another.

Challenge Options:

  • Beginner: Draw 10 cards.
  • Intermediate: Draw 15 cards.

Five health-related components describe how healthy you are. Six skill-related components describe how well you play. Name them, test them, and find your profile.

List All Six

List the six components of skill-related fitness and define each one in your own words:

speed · power · agility · balance · coordination · reaction time

assignments.title: Plank & Balance Challenge
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.10 · Fitness Components, Balance and Coordination
Week 22
🚀 Plank & Balance Flight Club

After exploring all 5 fitness components, train two at once: muscular strength + balance. The plank is the ultimate test of core endurance, and the variations layer on body control.

1
Your Goal

We're going to build strong muscles and endurance in your arms, core, and legs — all while having fun and learning to balance your body.

2
How to Play
  1. Get into a plank position: hands on the floor under your shoulders, body straight from your head to your toes, and tighten your tummy.
  2. Hold the plank for as long as you can while keeping good form.
    • Don't let your hips drop or lift too high.
    • Keep breathing!
  3. Stop when it gets too hard to keep your body straight.
  4. Try again later and see if you can hold it longer than before.
3
Try These Variations
  • Side Plank: Lie on your side and lift your body on one arm and the side of your foot. Switch sides after a few seconds.
  • Leg Lift Plank: Lift one leg while holding a plank. Switch legs every few seconds.
  • Partner Plank: Face a friend and try to hold your planks at the same time. Cheer each other on!
4
What You're Practicing
  • Muscles & Strength: Strong arms, shoulders, and core muscles
  • Endurance: Muscles that can work longer without getting tired
  • Balance & Control: Staying steady and moving safely

Tips:

  • Focus on quality over time — it's better to hold a good plank than a long, sloppy one.
  • Cheer your friends if you're in pairs or a group.
  • Beginners can try a knee plank or a forearm plank instead of the full plank.
✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

  • Time your max plank hold today. Identify the two fitness components it trains simultaneously. Then predict your hold time after 4 weeks of FITT-based plank training (specify your F, I, T, T).
  • Which energy system gave out first — and how did you know? Was it the burn (glycolytic), the breath (oxidative), or pure muscle quit (ATP-PC depleted)? Use the sensation as evidence.

assignments.title: Flight Club Wall Sit Countdown
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.11 · Rhythmic Movement and Dance
Week 24
🚀 Wall Sit Flight Club Countdown

Lower-body endurance test. Stand against a wall, slide down, and hold. It looks easy until the burn starts.

1
How to Play
  1. Find a clear wall space.
  2. Lean your back against the wall and slide down until your thighs are parallel to the floor, as if sitting in an invisible chair. Keep your knees directly above your ankles and your back flat against the wall.
  3. Hold this "chair" position for as long as you can, focusing on keeping good form.
2
Countdown Variation
  • Start by holding the position while counting down from a certain number (e.g., 30, 20, or 10 seconds).
  • Challenge yourself to reach zero without letting your thighs rise above parallel.
3
Difficulty Enhancements
  • Add a ball: Hold a small ball between your knees to engage inner thigh muscles.
  • Raise your hands: Extend your arms straight out in front of you or overhead to engage shoulders and core.
  • Single-leg lift: Carefully lift one foot off the ground for a few seconds, then switch legs to increase difficulty and balance challenge.
4
Safety Tips & Focus

Fitness Focus:

  • Muscular endurance: Keeps your thigh muscles working over time.
  • Strength: Strengthens quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and core.
  • Balance & focus: Helps improve stability and concentration while holding the position.

Safety Tips:

  • Avoid letting your knees go past your toes.
  • Keep your back flat against the wall.
  • Stop if you feel pain (muscle burn is okay, sharp pain is not).

Personal Challenge: Record how long you can hold the wall sit each day and try to improve your time. Think about which variations felt easiest or hardest and why.

✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

  • Time your max wall sit hold. Where did the burn show up first — quads, hamstrings, or glutes? That muscle is the limiter for this position. Design a 2-week strengthening plan for that specific muscle using FITT.
  • The wall sit holds for 30+ seconds at a steady moderate load — which energy system dominates? Compare to a 5-second max-effort jump (different system). Use duration and intensity to justify both classifications.

Paragraph 1
My Fitness Goal

Answer:

  • What is one fitness goal you want to improve over the next 30 days?
  • Why did you choose this goal?

My Personal Fitness Plan

  • Intensity: How hard will each session be?
  • Time: How long will each session last?
  • Type: Which specific exercises or activities?
  • How will you progressively overload from Week 1 to Week 4?
  • Who can help, coach, or check in on you?
  • How will you stay safe?

assignments.title: Training Cycle Implementation Log
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online

Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.13 · Goal Setting and Personal Fitness Plans
Week 25
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
PE.6.L.4.1PE.6.L.4.3HE.68.R.2.4HE.68.R.2.8HE.7.PHC.3.6

You wrote the plan. Now prove you ran it. A plan without an implementation record is a wish — this is the evidence half of "create, implement and assess."

1
Step 1
Restate the Plan and the Baseline

Copy in your SMART goal and FITT plan from My Fitness Goal & Plan, and record your starting measurement with the date. This is the number everything gets compared against.

2
Step 2
Log Every Session for Four Weeks

Keep a session log with one row per workout: date, activity, duration, intensity or load, how it felt (1–10), and any notes. Log the sessions you missed too, with the reason. The missed rows are data, not failures — they are what tells you whether the plan was realistic.

3
Step 3
Check In at the Halfway Point

At the end of week 2, re-measure your goal metric and record it. Write 2–3 sentences on whether you are on track, ahead, or behind.

4
Step 4
Adjust Using the Data

Based on your week-2 check-in, make one specific change to the plan. Name which FITT variable you changed, what you changed it to, and the reasoning. Remember the rule from the reading: if progress is slow, change the plan, not the goal.

5
Step 5
Handle the Setbacks

Something will get in the way — illness, homework, a busy week, losing motivation. Describe at least one real challenge or setback you hit and the strategy you used to manage it. Draw on at least two of: better time management, setting a realistic boundary, scaling the session down instead of skipping it, building in recovery, or asking someone for support.

6
Step 6
Assess the Cycle

Re-measure at four weeks. Report your baseline, week-2, and week-4 numbers, chart them, and answer: did the plan work? What is your evidence? Which single factor drove the result most — the training itself, your consistency, sleep, or nutrition? Then get a signature or short comment from your teacher, coach, or a parent who checked in with you during the cycle.

📝Weekly Reflection

Metacognition prompt: Look at your logged sessions against your planned sessions. What percentage did you actually complete? If it is below 80%, the honest question is not "was I lazy" but "was the plan built for the life I actually have?" Redesign one FITT variable so the plan would survive a genuinely busy week — and explain why a smaller plan you complete beats a bigger plan you abandon.

Optima
Academy Online

Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.13 · Goal Setting and Personal Fitness Plans
Spring Window

This is the spring window — your retest. You will run the exact same five-event FitnessGram battery you did in the fall, under the same conditions, and compare. A sport scientist controls the variables so the only real difference being measured is your training.

1
How It Works
Repeat the Battery — Same Conditions
  • Use the SAME space, surface, footwear, and timing app you recorded in the fall. Controlling these makes the comparison fair.
  • Run each event, self-report your numbers, and pull up your fall baseline to fill in the comparison.
  • As before, scores are compared to your Healthy Fitness Zone and to your OWN fall numbers — never to classmates. Your data stays private.
2
The Battery
The Same Five Events
EventWhat it measuresHow to run it at home
PACER (or One-Mile Run)Aerobic capacity — how well your heart and lungs deliver oxygen during sustained effort (estimated VO₂ max).Run the 20-meter PACER audio track in a measured space and count laps, or time yourself on a measured one-mile route.
Curl-UpAbdominal muscular strength and endurance.Do cadence curl-ups on a mat, counting in time with a cadence track. Film from the side if you can.
90° Push-UpUpper-body muscular strength and endurance.Do cadence push-ups, bending to a 90° elbow angle each rep. Film from the SIDE so form is visible.

Trunk LiftTrunk extensor strength and flexibility.Lie face down and lift your upper body slowly; have your helper measure your chin height from the floor with a ruler.

Score Sheet
Fall vs. Spring — Show the Change

Fill in your fall score, your new spring score, and the change (+ or −) for each event:

EventFall scoreSpring scoreChange
PACER laps (or mile time)__________________
Curl-Ups__________________
90° Push-Ups__________________
Sit-and-Reach (left / right)__________________
Trunk Lift__________________

Analyze your cycle with evidence:

  • Which events improved, and by how much? Which stayed flat or dropped?
  • For your focus event, what specific training do you think drove the change (or the lack of one)? Cite the FITT variable that mattered most.
  • If you ran another training cycle, what ONE thing would you change, and what is the mechanism behind that choice?

assignments.title: Myth vs. Fact: Marijuana and THC
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.12 · Substance Use and Abuse Prevention
Week 27
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
HE.68.SUA.3.3HE.68.SUA.5.3MA.K12.MTR.7.1ELA.K12.EE.1.1

Run the fact-versus-fallacy test on the substance with the most confident-sounding claims around it — then measure how wrong your own sense of "everyone" really is.

1
Step 1
Guess First, Then Look

Before you research anything, write down two predictions and do not change them later:

  • Out of 100 students your age, how many do you think used marijuana in the past year?
  • Out of 100 students your age, how many do you think vaped in the past month?

Now find the real, current numbers from a published survey — Monitoring the Future (monitoringthefuture.org) or the Florida Youth Substance Abuse Survey. Record the actual figures and cite where you found each one.

2
Step 2
Compute Your Error

For each prediction, subtract: your estimate minus the actual figure. That difference is your estimation error. Was it positive or negative? Answer in writing: which direction did you guess, and does that match what the reading said about pluralistic ignorance?

3
Step 3
Bust Four Myths

Take these four claims. For each one, state whether it is a myth or a fact, then give the accurate information and say where that information comes from.

  1. "It is natural, so it is safe."
  2. "You cannot get addicted to it."
  3. "Everyone our age is doing it."
  4. "It does not affect schoolwork or sports."

Name the Consequences

List five specific consequences of regular THC use for someone your age. At least one must be academic, one athletic, and one legal. For each, write one sentence on how it would interfere with a goal you actually wrote in your Unit 1.13 fitness plan.

📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: If most students overestimate how many of their peers use, what does that single wrong belief do to a person standing in a group being offered something? Design a one-sentence message that would correct the belief, and explain why your wording would land better with a 12- or 13-year-old than a poster that just says "don't do drugs."

assignments.title: Refusal Skills in Action
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online

Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.12 · Substance Use and Abuse Prevention
Week 28

A refusal is a skill, and skills are built by reps. You are going to write your lines, then actually say them out loud.

Step 1
Four Scenarios

For each of these four situations, write exactly what you would say — the actual words, in quotation marks — and name which refusal tool from the reading you used.

  1. At a gathering, an older student offers you a drink and says "one will not do anything."
  2. A friend you trust offers you a vape and says everyone on the team has tried it.
  3. Someone offers you a pill, saying it is "just" a prescription painkiller from their parent's cabinet.
  4. The ride home is with a driver you can tell has been drinking or using.
2
Step 2
Handle the Push-Back

For scenario 1 and scenario 2, write what you would say if the person does not accept your first no and pushes again. Remember the rule from the reading: say it once, then stop explaining. What does that look like in actual words?

3
Step 3
The Non-Negotiable One

Scenario 4 is different from the others. In 3–5 sentences, explain why the impaired-driver scenario has no version where the answer is yes, who else is affected by that choice besides you, and exactly what your alternative plan is — who you would call and how you would get home.

4
Step 4
Do the Reps

5
Step 5
Set Up Your Safety Net

Design prompt: Refusal works better when it is early, short, and steady. Take your weakest scenario — the one that felt hardest to write — and rewrite your response to be shorter. assignments.html:
Optima

Recognize an Overdose

2
Step 2
Recognize the Slower Signs

Overdose is sudden. Misuse over time looks different. List five signs that might suggest someone you know is misusing a substance, and mark which one you think would be easiest to miss in a friend — and why.

3
Step 3
Why Counterfeit Pills Change the Math

In 3–5 sentences, explain what fentanyl is, why a pill that did not come from a pharmacy cannot be assumed to be what it looks like, and what that means for the "it is just one prescription pill" argument.

4
Step 4
Three Sets of Rules

Make a three-column chart: Family rules, School rules, Florida law. Put at least two real entries in each column. For the law column, use the reading — for the school column, use your actual student code of conduct and athletic eligibility policy. If any part of this assignment is about you or someone you know right now, do not wait for a grade. Talk to your school counselor, or call or text 988, or call the SAMHSA Helpline at 1-800-662-HELP (4357) — free and confidential, any hour. In an emergency, call 911.

assignments.title: Take a Position: Defend It With Evidence
assignments.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
Grade 6/7 PE · Unit 1.12 · Substance Use and Abuse Prevention
Week 28
Florida Standards · M/J Comprehensive Physical Education Grade 6/7 (1508060)
HE.7.CEH.4.2ELA.K12.EE.1.1ELA.K12.EE.5.1ELA.K12.EE.6.1

Pick a side on a real health policy and defend it with accurate health information — not opinion, not vibes. This is the sport-scientist standard applied to an argument.

1
Step 1
Choose Your Issue

Choose ONE health-related issue and take a clear position on it:

  • Should the legal age to buy tobacco, nicotine and vape products be 21?
  • Should schools have a zero-tolerance policy for vaping on campus?
  • Should athletes who violate a substance policy lose eligibility for a season?
  • Should Florida keep its zero-tolerance BAC law for drivers under 21?
  • Should schools be required to teach about fentanyl and carry naloxone?
2
Step 2
State Your Position

Write one clear sentence stating your position. No hedging — a reader should know exactly where you stand.

3
Step 3
Support It With Health Information

Give three pieces of supporting evidence. Every one must be accurate health information with a named source — a health agency, a published survey, a statute, or your course readings. For each, write one sentence explaining how it supports your position. Personal opinion does not count as evidence here.

4
Step 4
Answer the Other Side

State the strongest argument against your position — stated fairly, the way someone who believes it would say it. Then respond to it with evidence. Taking the other side seriously makes your own argument stronger, not weaker.

5
Step 5
Deliver It

Present your position as a 1-page written argument, a 60–90 second video, or a one-slide infographic. Whatever the format, your position, your three evidence points, your counter-argument response, and your sources must all be visible.

📝Weekly Reflection

Set Up a Safe Space

Choose Your Elements

  • At least one roll (log, egg, forward, or shoulder)
  • At least two balances, each held a full 3 seconds, at different levels
  • At least one clear transfer of weight (for example feet to hands to feet)

Step 3
Map It

Write or draw your sequence in order. For each element, note the action type, the level (low / medium / high), and how it connects to the next one. Mark where you change level — you need at least two changes.

4
Step 4
Practise for Flow

Run it at least five times. You are chasing smoothness, not speed: no pauses to reset, no stumbles between elements. Add a steady beat or a song and try to match the tempo.

Perform and Record

Step 1
Find Your Partner or Group

Work with at least one other person — a classmate on a video call, a sibling, a parent, or a friend. If nobody is available in person, coordinate a synchronized routine over video and film both sides.

Step 2
Choose Your Apparatus

Pick at least one small apparatus (hoop, ball, rope, scarf or ribbon, beanbag) and, if you can do it safely, one large apparatus (a taped floor line as a beam, a mat, a sturdy low step, a bench). Household substitutions are listed in the reading. Nothing unstable, nothing you have to climb.

3
Step 3
Pick the Music and Find the Tempo

Choose a song and find its BPM (a free metronome or BPM-finder app will do it). Record the number. Decide how many beats each element of your routine will take — this is what keeps a group together.

4
Step 4
Build the Routine

Your routine must run at least 45 seconds and include:

  • At least three gymnastic actions (balance, roll, weight transfer, or a held shape)
  • At least three forms of locomotion moving on or around the apparatus

5

Rehearse and Perform

⚠️Safety & Support

Apparatus adds risk. Keep the small apparatus under control and away from faces. Never place a large apparatus on a slippery surface, and never use furniture as apparatus. Agree on spacing before you start — two people swinging a rope or hoop need more personal space than either would alone. That is the same spatial-awareness principle that keeps a shared activity space safe.

Timing prompt: Where in the routine did your group fall out of sync most often? Was it a fast section, a slow section, or a transition? quizzes.title: Quiz 5: Teamwork, Fitness Components, Balance & Goals

questions.text: Sara plays soccer 3 days a week and does push-ups every morning. Which TWO fitness components is she training the MOST?

answers.text: Flexibility and body composition.
Cardiovascular endurance and muscular strength.
Balance and coordination only.
Speed and reaction time only.

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST SMART fitness goal?

answers.text: I want to be in shape someday.
I want to be the fastest runner in school by the end of next week.
I will run a mile in under 9 minutes by April 30, by jogging 20 minutes three times a week.
I want to never feel tired again.

questions.text: When you balance on one foot, your body uses THREE sources of information to stay steady. Which is NOT one of them?

answers.text: Your eyes (vision).
Your inner ear (which detects head motion).
Sensors in joints and muscles (proprioception).
Your sense of smell.

questions.text: A team where every member feels safe speaking up, admitting mistakes, and trying new ideas is more likely to succeed than a team that only listens to its loudest player — researchers call this 'psychological safety.'

answers.text: True
False

questions.text: What is the term for the training-plan strategy where coaches alternate phases of building strength, building speed, building endurance, and recovery so the athlete peaks at the right time? (One word.)

answers.text: periodization

questions.text: Before a game, some teammates pressure Jordan to skip the warm-up to 'look tough,' while another teammate insists the group warm up together to avoid injury. Which statement about peer pressure is correct?

answers.text: All peer pressure is negative and should be ignored.
Peer pressure can be positive (the warm-up teammate raising the standard) or negative (the skip-the-warm-up group lowering it).
Only adults can create peer pressure.
Peer pressure has no real effect on athletes' choices.

questions.text: A new teammate is still learning a skill the rest of the team already has. Which response best shows respect for different ability levels AND strengthens the team?

answers.text: Call them 'the weak link' so they practice harder.
Leave them out of drills until they catch up on their own.
Adjust the activity so they can contribute while they improve, and encourage their progress.
Only pass to the most skilled players so the team wins faster.

questions.text: After a stressful week, which choice is the BEST example of using movement for stress management — and the correct reason why?

answers.text: Sitting still and worrying, because rest alone always lowers stress.
A 15-minute dance or rhythmic-movement session, because rhythmic movement lowers cortisol and releases mood-lifting endorphins.
Skipping all activity until the stress passes on its own.
Eating a large meal, because food is the only real stress reliever.

questions.text: Coach Lin has a 12-year-old athlete who wants to be a better all-around basketball player. Her current weaknesses on the team are: she fatigues by the third quarter (cardio limiter), she gets crossed over easily by faster guards (agility limiter), and she rolls her ankle a lot (balance/proprioception limiter). (1) Write a SMART goal for this athlete that targets all three limiters over a 60-day window. (2) Apply the FITT principle and design a weekly training plan with at least one training day for each limiter. (3) Identify ONE specific data point Coach Lin should measure on Day 60 to prove the plan worked. (4) Name ONE piece of technology (a fitness app, wearable, video, or spreadsheet) Coach Lin could use to assess, design, or evaluate the plan, and state exactly what data it would provide.

quizzes.description: Final nine questions covering Modules 1.10 to 1.13. Includes teamwork, respecting diverse abilities, peer pressure, sportsmanship, the 5 fitness components, balance, safety, stress management, SMART goals, and periodization.

questions.text: Alcohol is classified as a depressant. What does that actually mean for the body?

answers.text: It makes a person feel sad or depressed.
It slows down the central nervous system, including reaction time, coordination, and breathing.
It speeds up the heart so an athlete performs better.
It only affects the liver and nothing else.

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST description of why fentanyl has made counterfeit pills so dangerous?

answers.text: Counterfeit pills always taste different, so they are easy to identify.
Fentanyl is far more potent than most opioids, and an amount too small to see can be a lethal dose in a pill made to look real.
Fentanyl only appears in pills sold in other countries.
Counterfeit pills are dangerous only if you take more than five of them.

answers.text: The exit and the code word.
The reason and the redirect.
The ally and the plain no.

questions.text: You find a friend unresponsive, breathing very slowly, with blue-gray lips. What is the FIRST thing you should do?

Call 911 immediately, stay with them, and tell the dispatcher you think it is an overdose.
Drive them somewhere yourself without telling an adult.
Give them coffee and walk them around the room.

It only matters for adults, not for students.
It makes surveys impossible to conduct.

questions.text: In an invasion sport such as soccer or basketball, what are ALL offensive strategies fundamentally trying to do?

answers.text: Keep possession without ever advancing the ball.
Create space, then use it before the defense closes it.
Make sure only the most skilled player touches the ball.
Slow the game down so nobody has to run.

questions.text: A team plays zone defense. What is the predictable trade-off they are accepting?

answers.text: It protects the middle and saves energy, but concedes space in the seams between zones.
It has no weaknesses, which is why every team uses it.

answers.text: Your center of gravity has moved outside your base of support.

Move to the middle of the field, away from the trees, and continue.

discussions.title: Data Review: Compare Your Numbers and Your Reasoning
discussions.html:
All year you have been collecting numbers on your own body - resting heart rate, recovery rate, plank hold, toe-touch reach, mile time, FitnessGram scores, vision-dependency gap. This thread is where we do what sport scientists actually do with data: compare it, argue about it, and explain our reasoning to each other.

Your first post. Pick ONE measurement you tracked more than once. Post:

  • The measurement, your baseline number, and your most recent number
  • The change, and the exact conditions you tested under both times
  • Your explanation of why it changed or did not - the mechanism, not just "I trained more"
  • One reason your own data might be misleading

Your replies (at least two). This is the part that counts:

  • Find a classmate who measured the same thing. Compare methods, not scores - did you test under the same conditions? Whose method was more controlled, and why?
  • Respectfully challenge one explanation in the thread. Could something else account for the change - sleep, growth, measurement error, a different surface or time of day? Offer an alternative explanation and say what evidence would settle it.
  • If someone challenges your reasoning, respond with evidence rather than defending. Being wrong about a mechanism is normal; that is why we compare.

Ground rules. We compare methods and reasoning, never bodies. Nobody's number is better or worse than anyone else's - FitnessGram is criterion-referenced and personal for exactly this reason. Do not rank, do not comment on anyone's body, and do not post anyone else's data.

To close: post a final comment naming one thing you would measure differently next time because of something a classmate said.

discussions.title: Advocacy Campaign: Building a Substance-Free Standard Together
discussions.html:
This is a group build, not a solo post. Together we are going to design a real substance-free advocacy campaign for students our age — the kind that works because it comes from us and not from a poster in a hallway.

Your first post (by midweek). Bring one of these three:

  • A message: one sentence you think would actually land with a 6th or 7th grader. Say who it is aimed at and why you think it would work.
  • A fact: one accurate, sourced piece of health information the campaign should use — especially a real prevalence number that corrects the "everyone is doing it" belief.
  • A format: where and how the campaign should reach people (a locker-room sign, a short video, a morning announcement, a team pledge) and why that format fits the audience.

Your replies (at least two, by the end of the week). This is where the cooperative work happens, so make them count:

  • Build on a classmate's idea — add something concrete that makes it stronger.
  • Ask a genuine question about a claim, or respectfully push on whether a message would really work with the audience it is aimed at.
  • If you disagree, disagree with the idea and not the person, and say what you would do instead.

Ground rules. Use accurate information and say where it came from. Do not name or describe any real person's substance use, including your own or a family member's — keep it about the campaign. Listen for the quiet ideas; the reading was clear that the best teams surface them on purpose.

To close: after reading the thread, post a short final comment naming one idea from someone else that changed your thinking, and what you would put on the campaign if we could only use one message.

discussions.title: Culture and Play: What the World Invented
discussions.html:
We each played a different game this week. This thread is where the class turns eleven separate experiences into one shared map of what movement looks like around the world.

Your first post. Introduce the game you played. Include:

  • Its real name, where it comes from, and one thing you learned about its history or significance that surprised you
  • The one skill it demanded most - and be specific, not "coordination"
  • The hardest moment, and what your body could not do at first
  • One adaptation you made, and whether it changed the game for better or worse

Your replies (at least two).

  • Reply to someone who played a different game from yours. Ask a real question about how it works, or about the culture it came from.
  • Find a classmate whose game shares a skill with yours. Name the shared skill and work out together which sport both would transfer into.

Listening matters here. Some classmates may be writing about a game from their own family's culture. Read carefully, use the real names of games and places, ask questions with genuine curiosity, and do not make a culture into a punchline. If someone shares something personal, respond to the person before you respond to the information.

To close: post a final comment naming one game from the thread you want to try, and one thing a classmate said that changed how you think about why different places invented different games.
